data.title: Stop clutching your pearls over state capitalism. It never went away
data.description:
The reaction of Right-wing pundits to the US government’s extraordinary intervention in Venezuelan oil has been predictably alarmist. But it shouldn’t be.

Far from signalling the end of capitalism or democracy, it’s the clearest sign yet that the West is finally prepared to do whatever it takes to protect the free world from authoritarian rivals that have learned to exploit its openness against it.

Under the emerging arrangement, the Pentagon – acting through the Biden-created Office of Strategic Capital (OSC) – is taking a direct stake in a venture controlling huge Venezuelan oil concessions to encourage American companies back into the country.

That may sound strikingly conflicting given the free-market norms that have governed the West’s economic order since the Reagan and Thatcher era.

But dig deeper, and one realises that the laissez-faire system we thought we had may never have been quite as entrenched as we thought.

To a lesser or greater degree, the influence of the state has always been present in commerce and markets, particularly when vital national interests are at stake.

Nick Butler, Gordon Brown’s former energy adviser who once managed BP’s relationship with the British government, provided a telling example of this fact on a panel about the rise of state capitalism at a finance festival earlier this year. He recalled how Tony Blair had one day summoned him to No 10 to advise that BP should invest in Russia as a matter of government policy. BP duly did.

For Butler, therefore, there is nothing particularly surprising about the US government becoming increasingly interventionist in trade, commerce or markets. “I think it is entirely natural,” he told the audience.

“There is a mutual relationship of mutual benefit between the two. It may not always be as transparent as it should be, but I think it’s there.”

He reiterated the point to me this week. “Energy is too important for governments to leave to the free market because it represents such an important part of economic life and therefore of national security,” he said.

Seen in this light, the national-security apparatus has always reserved the right to override the normal conventions of liberal government when vital interests are threatened. This includes on a contingency basis, as is happening now.

What is changing, therefore, is not the relationship itself but its visibility: what was previously implicit, and often conducted behind closed doors, is essentially becoming explicit as national security threats deepen.

Nor is this merely an American phenomenon. Andy Burnham this week signalled that Britain too will move towards greater public control of essential services to protect its sovereign capacity in strategic sectors including energy, steel and defence.

For those on the Right, the knee-jerk reaction, quite understandably, is to assume the worst: a Left-wing government is predictably indulging in the opportunity to over-extend itself into areas it has no business in.

Such an assumption may even have been fair historically. In the current context, however, it potentially misses the bigger picture. When sovereignty comes under threat, the interests of those seeking more government control increasingly align – at least temporarily – with those who prefer a freer system. In political theory, this is known as “the state of exception”.

We did not, after all, triumph in either World War under a free-market system.

In 1914, Winston Churchill, then the first lord of the admiralty, persuaded the government to buy a controlling stake in the Anglo-Persian Oil Company, BP’s predecessor, to secure fuel supplies for the Royal Navy. Moreover, the British government only disposed of its remaining BP shares in 1987.

The creation of the OSC in December 2022 is itself an explicit acknowledgement that capital allocation is becoming as strategically important as troop deployment. That’s why rather than rebel against the state-capitalism trend, investors, both in the UK and the US, would be better off recognising the value of joining in with patriotic investment flows.

Brent Johnson of Santiago Capital is among investors already doing so.

In a report published last year, he advised that the OSC’s published list of priorities should be viewed as an investment roadmap with the Pentagon’s list of target sectors acting as a “strategic map showing where the United States is most vulnerable and where private capital has underinvested relative to national security needs”.

The OSC’s job in that context is to “reduce risk for private investors” and crowd-in capital into those areas.

For investors, the signal could hardly be clearer: when the world’s most powerful government tells you which industries it considers indispensable to national survival, it may pay to listen.

This, however, is not just because we are going to see much more government involvement in markets as geopolitical fragmentation intensifies, it is because the comforting idea that Anglo-American capitalism ever operated entirely free of state direction was itself a misdirection. Especially when you consider the broader Western European context.

Even under the auspices of a supposedly free-market-championing EU, there has been far less anxiety in the Continent about displaying these dirigiste tendencies openly.

France, most obviously, has retained stakes in strategically important companies and industries from aerospace to energy. But even Brussels is now becoming more explicit, with Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, seeking to mobilise Europe’s vast pool of private savings into strategic sectors such as defence, while simultaneously pushing for greater European preference in strategic procurement.

That’s why, in Johnson’s view, it is better to understand the rise of the OSC, and its growing proximity to Wall Street, as the subtle unveiling of a “21st-century Manhattan Project” that has been operating in the background for some time. Its intent? To ensure that – when the time comes – private capital can and will be mobilised to finance the capabilities needed to compete with authoritarian challengers, both militarily and industrially.

Indeed, it’s also arguably why long before the OSC ever existed, there was In-Q-Tel. The CIA-backed venture was founded in 1999 and is behind technology superpowers like Palantir. Its creation arguably marked the moment the national-security establishment fully realised that innovation, particularly in information technology, would require the sort of commercial scale and private capital that could not be replicated behind classified walls.

To maintain its edge, government would need to seed the strategic capabilities it might one day need to draw increasingly in plain sight.

The OSC is the logical extension of that strategy.

Britain’s own versions of this machinery, the National Security Strategic Investment Fund and Advanced Research and Invention Agency, did not arrive until 2018 and 2023 respectively. They have, consequently, had far less time to shape the investment landscape.

But since the structures are now in place and their purpose is becoming clearer, investors should no longer delay getting on board. Putting capital behind the technologies and industrial capacity that defend the strategic autonomy of Britain and its allies is no longer merely patriotic. It is where governments themselves are telling us the money will flow.

data.title: Britain’s gas cliff-edge is drawing dangerously close
data.description:
“Britain will control its own energy rather than depending on markets controlled by petrostates and dictators,” said Ed Miliband just before Labour won the 2024 election.

He was pledging to break the growing grip of countries ranging from Norway and the US to Qatar and Algeria on Britain’s energy supplies. Labour promised to replace imported oil and gas with low-carbon alternatives such as nuclear power, wind farms and solar plants.

Two years later, Britain faces a cliff edge in gas supplies, surging prices and soaring imports. This winter looks bad enough. Centrica’s Rough facility, the UK’s only major gas store, is facing the threat of closure without government support, and European storage levels are at their lowest in years.

Analysts are warning of January price increases on top of the 4pc increase planned in October and the 13pc rise last July.

But in a few years, they warn, the situation could be far worse because the UK’s North Sea output is plummeting faster than ever expected.

Last year the North Sea produced 28 billion cubic metres (bcm) of gas – 41pc of Britain’s needs. But in four years, that will have halved to just 14 bcm. And by 2035 it will more than halve again, to 6 bcm.

That reduction could be mitigated by approving new fields such as Jackdaw and Rosebank – but not by much. And those raw figures, from the North Sea Transition Authority, the government regulator, are increasingly striking fear into the gas industry, energy suppliers and government ministers.

They imply that the UK faces increasingly tough, expensive and potentially cold winters over the next decade, and that Britain’s reliance on petrostates will be greater than ever.

“The gap between demand and supply is widening, and it’s going to widen even further in the coming years,” said Iryna Sereda, the global head of gas and LNG at BloombergNEF. “In 10 years, two thirds of the UK’s gas production will be gone.

“Demand is falling too, but not nearly so fast, which means the UK will become increasingly dependent on imports.

“By 2030 it’s likely to be above 70pc and by 2035, we could be as high as 85pc dependent on imports.”

That growing gap between North Sea supplies and UK demand will have to be filled. The only way to do that is by liquefied natural gas (LNG), all of which will have to be imported.

The US is Britain’s main supplier of LNG, but we also buy increasing amounts from Qatar, Egypt, Algeria, China, Equatorial Guinea and Turkey – all of them authoritarian states. And last year alone LNG imports rose 24pc.

So as North Sea output declines, the UK’s hopes of breaking away from “petrostates and dictators” look likely to go into reverse. How did a country that was once self-reliant in energy end up in such a mess? And have ministers even realised?

Gas stockpile plans

One sign that they are waking up came last month when it emerged that Miatta Fahnbulleh, the new Energy Secretary, is considering plans to acquire a large ship that would become the UK’s newest LNG import terminal.

The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero also confirmed plans to create a government-controlled stockpile of natural gas that could be drawn on in emergencies.

Both schemes recognise that the Government’s plans to reduce our reliance on gas are faltering, leaving the UK at increasing risk of price spikes and shortages.

Recently published North Sea Transition Authority data show the physical reality of the North Sea decline.

The UK has about 172 offshore gas fields operating in 2026, but by 2030 around 62 are scheduled to close, leaving just 110. By 2035, another 40 will be gone.

Some of that decline is natural. The North Sea is a mature basin, and output was gently falling by about 5pc a year up until 2022.

But after Rishi Sunak’s government adopted Miliband’s policy of a windfall tax, the annual decline surged to around 15pc as offshore operators scrambled to quit the North Sea.

That could get even worse. If, for example, John Healey carries out his threat to extend the windfall tax, many more North Sea fields would become uneconomic and shut down.

But it’s not just the UK’s own North Sea decline that it should be worrying about.

‘Norway is vital’

Norway, the supplier of about a third of the UK’s gas, is facing the same problem of natural decline.

Britain’s gas needs are not constant. They rise and fall with the seasons. But in the winter, when demand is highest, up to 90pc of the gas burnt in the UK is Norwegian.

That reliance is becoming a problem. A report from the Norwegian Offshore Directorate warns that Norway’s oil and gas supplies peaked last year at around 230 bcm and are expected to plummet to as low as 110 million cubic metres by 2035.

Nikolai Astrup, a Norwegian MP and a key figure on its parliament’s finance committee, said the UK should already be looking for new energy sources. He says: “Right now, Norway is Europe’s largest and most predictable supplier of gas, and all the gas and oil we produce is sold to the UK and Europe. Norway is therefore vital to European energy security.

“But it is a geological fact that the Norwegian Shelf is mature and that the fall in production will be very sharp from 2035 onwards.”

One solution is to reduce demand – an approach recommended by Seb Kennedy, of market data specialist Energy Flux. He argues that building more LNG import facilities would make the UK unhealthily reliant on imports.

He says: “Rather than expanding LNG import facilities, the UK should focus on measures that reduce demand, such as fast-tracking heat pump deployment, investing in heat networks and supporting homeowners with insulation costs.”

That sounds like a solution – until you look at the latest government data. Forecasts of falling gas demand are based on householders installing 600,000 heat pumps a year, mostly to replace old boilers.

But the reality is that 125,000 heat pumps were sold per year, only 7pc of the heating market, dwarfed by the 1.7 million gas and oil boilers purchased.

Gas consumption has fallen in other areas – but not necessarily in ways that benefit Britain. Industrial consumption has plummeted from 19 bcm in 2000 to 8 bcm last year – linked to the closure of thousands of factories.

But the reductions in demand from those shutdowns – and the corresponding displacement of gas-fired power generation by renewables – are nowhere near as fast as the looming decline in UK and Norwegian supplies.

‘Increasingly fragile’

ICIS, a commodity-market consultancy, has modelled the risks posed by this growing gas supply and warns that the winter of 2028-29 is when the threat could become real.

Organisations such as the National Energy System Operator always point to the UK’s diverse gas-supply sources as its best defences.

Those sources include North Sea output, piped imports from Norway, three LNG terminals, interconnector pipelines with Belgium and the Netherlands, and storage.

But ICIS analysis points out that with three of those sources in decline – the North Sea, Norway and storage – the UK is at increasing risk.

“Great Britain’s and Ireland’s security of gas supply becomes increasingly fragile under a declining trajectory of UK natural gas production,” it says.

“Under normal conditions, peak demand can be met, with spare capacity remaining ... In reality, however, each supply source is exposed to planned and unplanned outages.

“The loss of Norwegian imports, or the shutdown of either of the UK’s two large LNG terminals (Isle of Grain or South Hook) significantly reduces available supply.

“If this happens, supply fails to meet demand, not only on the peak demand day but also on multiple days across both the 2028-2029 winter and the preceding winter.”

Some experts say the UK’s and Norway’s decline in gas production matters little because global LNG supplies are growing fast enough to replace it.

David Luff, of Argus Media, said: “Over the next five years, UK gas production is expected to decline faster than consumption, increasing the reliance on imports. But this import dependence will coincide with a significant expansion in global LNG supply, driven primarily by new export capacity in North America and Qatar.”

“Ofgem backs that up. LNG imports will play an important balancing role, although competition for cargoes could intensify if global markets tighten,” said a spokesman.

In other words, far from breaking free from petrostates, Britain will become increasingly reliant on them.

Andrew Bowie, the shadow energy secretary, said the growing reliance on imported energy was exactly the opposite of what the Government had promised before the election.

“The UK cannot continue to refuse to produce our own energy,” he says. “Labour’s ban on new licences, the windfall tax and delays in approving new fields like Jackdaw and Rosebank have put our energy security at risk. We need to get Britain drilling again.”

data.title: John Lewis suffers worst losses since pandemic after Labour tax raid
data.description:
John Lewis has fallen to its worst loss since the pandemic as the department store chain took a hit from Labour’s National Insurance tax raid.

The retailer, which also owns Waitrose supermarkets, reported a loss before tax of £124m in the first half of the year, compared with £88m a year earlier.

John Lewis blamed a rise in operating costs after Labour’s increase to employers’ National Insurance contributions.

It also pointed to higher investment in its stores, while shoppers held back on making larger purchases as the rising cost of living took its toll.

It is the retailer’s worst pre-tax loss since the first six months of 2020, when lockdown drove John Lewis £634m into the red.

Jason Tarry, the chairman of the John Lewis Partnership, said: “Our first-half results reflect our continued investment in our transformation, a more challenging trading environment and the increased costs of doing business.

“We are managing the business with discipline and have chosen to keep investing in our customers, partners and the long-term strength of our brands. While losses grew in the half, our employee-owned model allows us to take that longer-term view, supported by our financial strength.”

Mr Tarry, the former boss of Tesco, said he was “confident” that the partnership would make a profit for the year as a whole but added that consumer confidence remained fragile.

He said: “Customers are undoubtedly more cautious about spending, particularly on bigger ticket items in their homes.”

Mr Tarry blamed the rising cost of living – particularly higher fuel prices – as well as the conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East and concerns about household debt and interest rates for the tough trading conditions.

He added: “People may have been holding back for the interest rate reductions earlier in the year that don’t seem to be happening.”

However, he insisted the group remained committed to its huge “long-term, multi year” investment programme – including refurbishment of ageing department stores – aimed at boosting revenue and profitability.

Investment was up 30pc to £246m in the first half of the year and will hit £600m for the financial year as a whole.

Mr Tarry also called on John Healey, the Chancellor, to “deliver against the manifesto pledge” to reform business rates.

“They are the biggest business tax we face and in some locations, it’s our biggest single cost,” he said.

Sales at Waitrose rose 4pc to £4.3bn thanks to increased demand for its own-brand range and growth in online shopping.

However, operating profit fell by £7m as the supermarket racked up extra costs during recent heatwaves and invested in loyalty schemes and price cuts.

Sales fell 2pc at John Lewis department stores as customers tightened their belts, with the retailer cutting prices to offset lower demand.

Overall, revenues rose 2pc to £6.3bn in the first half of the year. Bosses warned they were cautious about the outlook for the second half of the year – which usually accounts for the majority of profit – because of ongoing economic and geopolitical uncertainty.

The first-half slump in sales represents John Lewis’s deepest losses excluding a Covid-induced slump in 2020, when it lost £635m in six months.

Mr Tarry warned staff in July of “really tough” trading conditions and the company racked up exceptional costs of £35m as it cut head office jobs.

Peter Ruis, the former managing director of the John Lewis department stores, who left last week, said a sense of “perma-crisis” was leading its customers to defer spending.

The scale of the loss will raise concerns among the group’s 66,000 employee partners about what level of bonus it will be able to afford to pay staff at the end of the year.

The bonus returned at 2pc last year – equivalent to an extra week’s pay – after being scrapped for three years.

It emerged last week that Mr Tarry had drawn up a three-year turnaround plan for the department store codenamed “Rise” in an effort to generate hundreds of millions of pounds of extra profit.

Since taking over from Dame Sharon White two years ago, Mr Tarry has sought to simplify the partnership, dropping out of failed diversifications such as build-to-rent property developments.

data.title: Sadiq Khan’s net zero targets ‘will hit growth’
data.description:
Sir Sadiq Khan’s new net zero building rules threaten to restrict London’s growth, a leading property group has warned.

The London Property Alliance (LPA), which represents 400 investors and builders, said it was concerned that the Mayor of London’s plans to tighten the rules on carbon emissions for property developers could throttle economic activity in the capital, particularly in the City.

The group fears that the draft targets could effectively blocking the construction of new skyscrapers, preventing businesses from expanding and limiting investment.

Nikki Dibley, who chairs the LPA’s City Property Association (CPA) and is a senior executive at Helical, a London developer, said the carbon limits were “simply unrealistic” for tower blocks.

The Mayor has proposed capping the amount of carbon emissions for new offices, shops or warehouses to 605kg per sq metre. The targets cover embodied carbon, which means that emissions are measured both for the construction and eventual operation of the building.

At present, the average building constructed in central London emits 720kg of carbon per sq metre, though some more complex projects, such as skyscrapers, can emit much more.

The LPA pointed out that even the greenest towers built in London today would not meet Sir Sadiq’s standards. For example, an all-electric, low-carbon, 38-storey tower in the City of London has embodied carbon emissions of 681kg per sq metre.

“We are concerned that the proposed embodied carbon targets could constrain the delivery of tall buildings, with particular implications for growth in the City,” the property organisation wrote in an email to members.

The LPA said the targets will make it “substantially more difficult” to build towers bigger than 30 storeys, according to a study by engineering company Arup for the group.

Ms Dibley said: “The construction and development industries are very cognisant of the need to reduce carbon.

“It’s about making sure that [no unrealistic targets] are embedded in a plan that will be prohibitive to growth.”

The LPA said the industry has already shrunk its carbon emissions for London offices by around 24pc over the past five years, when compared with the benchmark set by the Mayor in 2021.

Ms Dibley added: “Demand for office space is increasing. That’s happening quite quickly. To substantiate that demand, we have to deliver the space that big international companies require.

“The quality and the availability of the buildings is essential in terms of underpinning London’s competitiveness and ability to attract domestic and international talent.

“But you can’t build towers everywhere. Because there are relatively limited areas, it’s important it [is] not unduly fettered by carbon targets that are simply unrealistic for buildings of that type.”

The LPA intends to raise its concerns with the Mayor’s office in a response to a consultation on Sir Sadiq’s strategy for London for the next two decades.

Ms Dibley said: “The City is the symbol of Britain’s finance centre. Being able to maintain, perpetuate and grow it, and ensure it has benefits not just for London, but for the UK as a whole, is really important.”

The proposed net zero targets pit Sir Sadiq’s claimed goals against the City of London’s desire to boost construction. The City of London Corporation’s draft plan seeks to add 1.2 million sq metres of office space by 2040, the majority of which would be delivered through skyscrapers.

Office space is currently in short supply in London, with just two new build offices in the capital bigger than 40,000 sq ft available to rent, according to separate data from Knight Frank. That is down from six last year.

A Mayor of London spokesman said the Greater London Authority engaged with the LPA before it published its draft plans and “look[s] forward to receiving” the property group’s response to the consultation.

data.title: TV remotes discriminate against Britain, say broadcasters
data.description:
Modern TV remotes are unfair because they discourage people from watching British programmes, broadcasters have claimed.

Everyone TV, a joint venture between the BBC, ITV, Channel 4 and Channel 5, has hit out at the growing number of sponsored buttons on remotes that link directly to streaming services such as Netflix and Amazon Prime.

The broadcasters argued that these shortcuts mean programmes from UK channels get buried under a mountain of choice from US rivals.

They warned that this would result in people tuning into British shows less frequently, which in term would undermine the “long-term viability” of the domestic industry.

Many manufacturers for streaming-only devices such as Amazon Fire TV have removed numbered and coloured buttons from their remotes altogether.

These have instead been replaced by an array of streaming shortcuts, alongside other features such as voice search.

TV manufacturers sell off valuable placements on their remotes, while search results from voice commands are often sponsored.

In addition to crowding out British TV, the broadcasters warned that modern remotes were leaving older and disabled viewers behind.

Everyone, which manages free-to-air TV through platforms including Freeview and Freely, said the cluttered and complex design presented “significant barriers” for less digitally adept viewers and those with disabilities.

Jonathan Thompson, the chief executive of Everyone TV, said: “As television moves into the streaming age, viewers should not have to relearn how to watch TV.

“Familiar features such as channel numbers, programme guides and intuitive remote controls have helped make television accessible to generations of viewers and remain just as important in a streaming world.”

In a submission to Ofcom, Everyone urged the regulator to introduce new rules forcing manufacturers to include easily identifiable and accessible numbered buttons, coloured buttons and a single, distinctive guide-button on remotes.

It also called for existing prominence rules, which require public service broadcasters to be clearly visible and accessible on the home screens of smart TVs, to be extended to include buttons.

TV bosses are understood to be pushing for a new “British TV” button to be installed on remotes, allowing viewers to navigate directly to programmes from UK channels. One suggested this button could bear a union flag.

The tussle over TV remotes comes amid an existential struggle for Britain’s public service broadcasters, which are grappling with an exodus of viewers to deep-pocketed US rivals and rival entertainment offerings from the likes of YouTube and TikTok.

The BBC is currently locked in negotiations with the Government over the future of the licence fee as it seeks to secure its long-term survival.

Matt Brittin, the new director general, is also fighting an internal revolt as he ploughs ahead with plans to slash as many as 2,000 jobs. In a call with staff this week, the BBC boss conceded that the broadcaster now faced a risk of strikes.

Commercial broadcasters are also grappling with a steep downturn in advertising revenues. Channel 4 this week announced plans to cut more than a quarter of its workforce, while ITV is in the process of selling its broadcasting arm to Sky in a £1.6bn deal aimed at building scale for the streaming age.

Ofcom said any reforms to TV remotes would require legislative change. The Government has already introduced new laws ensuring that British broadcasters are easily accessible on modern TV.

It is also consulting on plans to force social media sites such as YouTube, Facebook and X prominently display news from public service broadcasters.

However, the move has triggered concerns about censorship on both sides of the Atlantic after ministers refused to rule out requiring news publishers to sign up to a state-backed regulator in order to benefit from the measures.

data.title: The rise and fall of British helicopters
data.description:
Do you have a favourite helicopter? Mine, as a child, was Airwolf. But it could have been the helicopter that dropped Anneka Rice off at so many castles in the pioneering 1980s Channel 4 game-show Treasure Hunt, or the Blue Thunder choppers that ferry our elite SAS teams around Britain, tackling emergencies.

Today, in addition to their use by armed forces, they are status symbols for the 0.01 per cent. Donald Trump used to owned a fleet of three Sikorsky S-76 helicopters, with predictably gilded interiors. Yet not so long ago, some believed this form of transport would be used regularly by the hoi polloi; hopping into a chopper would be as common as hailing a black cab.

This month marks 40 years since the demise of British Airways Helicopters, and that brief moment in time when it seemed scheduled passenger helicopter services might actually catch on. So why did the helicopter never go truly mainstream?

Up in the Airlink

Focke-Wulf’s FW61 was unveiled in the 1930s, before Russian-American pioneer Igor Sikorsky took up the baton in the 1940s. The US company he founded would go on to dominate these machines’ development for half a century.

But passenger helicopter services actually began in the UK. The route? From Liverpool to Cardiff, launched by BEA in 1950, with an intriguing stop in Wrexham that would have suited Rob McElhenney and Ryan Reynolds if it were operating today.

More BEA routes followed, such as Birmingham to Northolt, and on to Heathrow. Birmingham got a pioneering “Rotorstation” for helicopters to land at. It was opened at Heybarnes Recreation Ground in Hay Mills – Peaky Blinders territory. Three flights left for London daily.

Between 1978 and 1986, a helicopter shuttle service, dubbed the Airlink, connected Gatwick and Heathrow. This was before the M25 was finished and when the journey between the two main London airports was tortuous. Helicopters ferried transit passengers from apron to apron in minutes.

A vision of the future

The thinking among many was that helicopters would be omnipresent. During the Festival of Britain, there was a helicopter landing pad on the Southbank in London. The Southbank was earmarked for a more permanent heliport, which explains the brutalist design of the Queen Elizabeth Hall. It was supposed to protect against the noise and vibrations of helicopters.

In the end a heliport at Battersea was opened, further along the River Thames, and is still in use today. Architects’ designs for Sixties new towns always showed two things: a monorail, and helicopters fluttering in the sky. This was the vision of the future – back when we believed in a future that would be better.

Even the GPO became enamoured with helicopters and trialled their use to deliver post to the rural towns of Norfolk. Quite what Farmer Giles, drinking a pint of warm Bullard’s outside The Railway Inn in Docking on a Sunday afternoon in 1948, would have made of the sight of a GPO Sikorsky S-51 on a post run to Wells-Next-The-Sea is anyone’s guess.

In the Fifties, Britain ramped up its own helicopter production at Westland’s Yeovil site, which became the home of the British helicopter. The Dragonfly, Widgeon, Whirlwind and Wessex became instantly recognisable machines built in Somerset. The Sea King, Wasp and Scout followed, then it was into the era of more modern machines like the Puma, Gazelle and Lynx.

Away with the Faireys

Among the more bizarre ideas was the Fairey Rotodyne: a hybrid between a plane and a helicopter that doesn’t look a million miles away from the stretched fuselage of the Chinook. In 1959 it flew from Heathrow to Paris via Dover and Brussels, but it wouldn’t catch on. One of the problems was the immense noise its rotors generated. This was going to be a problem when it was clattering over the roofs of densely populated areas of South London on the way to Battersea Heliport.

Westland took over Fairey in the 1960s, but domestic helicopter production was to become a hot political potato. Britain’s varied and incredibly successful aerospace entities were walking a tightrope between innovating, investing, exporting and balancing the books. Their designs were legendary, but of course not everything worked. There was always a tussle between nationalising everything into what would become British Aerospace and selling parts off to foreign investors.

Westland became a political football during the so-called Westland Affair in 1985, which pitted different factions of Margaret Thatcher’s Conservative government against each other, as arguments raged over whether to maintain this facility in Yeovil, who should run it and who would pay for it.

End of an era

Why did helicopters fade away? As with other futuristic transport ideas like hovertrains, monorails, hovercraft and other “gadgetbahns”, their relatively high cost and niggling technical problems could never be fully resolved.

Aeroplanes, trains and cars driving on motorways won the transport arms race because they could be easily scaled, and eventually mass uptake drastically reduced costs. These forms of transport made money rather than costing it.

Motorways connect us. With the M40 complete, there was no need to take a helicopter from Birmingham to London. Helicopters are also gas guzzlers – even Porsche owners would baulk at the price of a full tank. Sabena wanted to follow the Rotodyne’s first international flight and start a helicopter from London to Brussels – but Eurostar does that journey more efficiently.

In the US, where traffic is terrible and public transport is worse, Blade has put up a fight, offering relatively affordable flights from JFK to Manhattan, but without the drama of the former Pan Am helicopter, which whisked passengers to the top of the Pan Am HQ in Midtown in the 1960s.

Helicopters are still popular as niche forms of transport, and incredibly useful for medical evacuations, police and military use, and VIP transport. UK Air Sea Rescue has used helicopters to rescue the lives of countless sailors around our shores, and helicopters have ferried thousands of workers to oil and gas rigs in the North Sea and beyond, from Aberdeen, Norwich, Humberside and other hubs.

But their mass-market use has dwindled in the face of competition – which is sad, because they have a real value. The experience of being in one is not like regular flying because you’re so low you can see everything below you. The feeling of rising into the sky for the first time is surreal.

Rare survivors

The Scilly Isles are one of the rare examples of a route where helicopters make sense, and these flights have continued on and off from 1964 to this day. My honeymooning parents cannot have been the only holidaymakers caught out by rough seas who needed to use the helicopter as a way to swiftly get off the islands. For locals, they are a lifeline back to the shops, schools and health services of Penzance. This is now the last surviving scheduled British helicopter service.

Nice to Monaco and Saint-Tropez are other popular services going strong, as are Helity’s routes from Malaga and Algeciras to the headline-grabbing Spanish exclave of Ceuta. Hong Kong to Macau is another example. Faroese flag carrier Atlantic Airways runs domestic helicopter flights. But anyone who’s gone puffin-spotting in Mykines, and found themselves stuck on the island for days due to bad weather, will know that helicopters aren’t much use in storms or low visibility, which is pretty much every day in a Faroe Islands winter.

For the super-rich class there will always be helicopters ready to take them to the British Grand Prix or Goodwood (two of the biggest weekends for the Battersea Heliport). But for the rest of us, the dream of flying everywhere by helicopter is elusive. It’s not impossible though – this is why helicopter aficionados specifically head to Tresco or Tórshavn.

data.title: Canned supermarket ‘mackerel’ has ‘no real mackerel’
data.description:
Supermarkets are selling cans of “mackerel” that contain none of the Atlantic-caught oily fish, replacing it with an imported species that critics claim tastes like “cheap tuna”.

Tesco, Sainsbury’s and Lidl are now selling tins labelled as “Jack mackerel”, supplied by food manufacturer Princes, which switched its supplies of Atlantic mackerel to fish caught off the coast of Chile last year.

Despite sharing a name, Chilean Jack mackerel is not from the same family as the mackerel caught off the coasts of the UK and typically sold in supermarkets. Jack mackerel has a meatier texture than mackerel, a different taste and around half the Omega-3.

Princes said its mackerel was “clearly identified”.

It comes as concerns about mackerel supplies in the Atlantic force supermarkets to swap out the fish for alternatives. Waitrose stopped selling fresh mackerel earlier this year because of sustainability concerns. It is currently phasing out its tinned mackerel stocks.

While Sainsbury’s and Tesco are still selling some Scottish and North Atlantic fish, Princes’ products are now also being stocked. Tesco has also announced plans to swap its own-brand tins of mackerel for Jack mackerel.

Some tins of Jack mackerel in Lidl are marketed alongside promotions for “mackerel” in stores, according to the Financial Times.

Hugo Tagholm, the chief executive of the marine charity Oceana, said: “The decision to stock Jack mackerel is because of the poor state of the mackerel population around the UK. They are really struggling.

“Supermarkets are really getting ahead because of the need to build our mackerel stocks.”

However, some fish aficionados have criticised canned Jack mackerel for its taste and smell.

According to a video by Marcus Ansell, a seafood reviewer with 650,000 followers on Instagram, Jack mackerel is “not even real mackerel” and “smells rather metallic ... just like cheap rubbish tuna”.

The International Council for the Exploration of the Sea earlier this year recommended a 70pc decrease in the UK’s mackerel catch limit from 576,958 tonnes to just 174,357 tonnes.

Supplies of mackerel have fallen by about three quarters in the past decade because of overfishing and waning plankton stocks.

While the UK has cut its mackerel catch quota, other countries continue to pillage stocks of the fish.

Russia, which has no mackerel of its own, was told this year its fishermen should catch up to 1,500 tonnes, but officials set their own limit at 67,000 tonnes.

Warmer seas have also seen plankton move further north, leading to greater fish stocks in Icelandic and Faroese waters, who have demanded greater quotas.

Tinned fish, once seen as a cheap option, has become popular among Gen Z foodies in recent years, and a number of luxury tinned fish businesses have entered the market.

A Princes Group spokesman said: “Princes took the decision to move its branded range away from North-East Atlantic mackerel, following years of concern over unsustainable catch levels and insufficient progress towards a science-based management agreement.

“We chose Marine Stewardship Council [MSC] certified Chilean Jack mackerel as an independently certified sustainable alternative, following extensive product and consumer testing.

“The species is clearly identified on our products, and we would consider sourcing North-East Atlantic mackerel again if sustainable management is restored and MSC certification regained.”

Lidl said it was “committed to sourcing fish and seafood from responsibly managed fisheries”.

Tesco and Sainsbury’s were contacted for comment.

data.title: Volkswagen faces ‘more than critical’ crisis, warns carmaker’s boss
data.description:
Volkswagen’s chief executive has warned that the crisis facing the German carmaker is “more than critical”, urging employees to brace for “the biggest upheaval in their history”.

Oliver Blume said US tariffs, the war in the Middle East and mounting competition from China had all contributed to a downturn that threatens to worsen in the coming years.

In an internal memo seen by The Telegraph, he said that Volkswagen’s current profits were “by no means sufficient” for it to continue investing in “new technologies, new products and our locations”.

He added that “we have to assume that risks will get worse, worldwide”, claiming that “we are in the biggest transformation in the history of the global automotive industry”.

His comments form part of efforts to win over staff as part of a controversial turnaround plan, which could include closing four of its German factories and laying off as many as 100,000 workers.

The company’s brands include Audi, Porsche and Škoda.

Mr Blume said that “Chinese manufacturers are pushing aggressively into Europe” and selling cars at “price points we cannot match”.

He added that he could not see any way Volkswagen’s factories in Emden, Hannover, Zwickau and Neckarsulm could remain profitable into the next decade.

The carmaker’s chief said Volkswagen’s overheads were “still around 30pc above the level of comparable companies”, adding: “We cannot carry that disadvantage indefinitely and must reduce it.”

Volkswagen made history in December last year by closing its Dresden plant. This was the first time the carmaker had shut one of its German factories in its 88-year history.

Mr Blume said Volkswagen was also exploring “industrial solutions” to keep its factories running, as he suggested that shutting factories would be “the last and most expensive solution”.

He highlighted the potential to convert Volkswagen’s Osnabrück plant into a production facility for Israeli firm Rafael Advanced Defense Systems, with the aim of saving 2,300 jobs.

Volkswagen first announced plans to cut 50,000 jobs in 2024.

However, the restructuring led to a fierce backlash from Germany’s powerful trade unions who have led protests at its factories across the country.

Mr Blume said Volkswagen had already reached agreements with around 37,000 staff to cut jobs, primarily through early retirement deals.

The carmaker warned last year that Donald Trump’s tariffs would inflict a €5bn- (£4.4bn) a-year hit on its business.

data.title: Poundstretcher’s US owner plots deal for Poundland
data.description:
The owner of Poundstretcher is exploring a potential deal for Poundland in a takeover that could unite two of Britain’s biggest budget high street chains.

The Telegraph has learned that Fortress Investment Group is in talks with Gordon Brothers, which bought Poundland in a £1 rescue deal just over a year ago, over a potential tie-up.

Sources said that advisers at Alvarez and Marsal were engaging with Fortress alongside a handful of other interested parties.

Options for the business also include a potential management buyout.

Discussions between Gordon Brothers and Fortress, a US fund that is majority owned by Abu Dhabi’s Mubadala Capital, are believed to be at an early stage.

It is understood that Fortress is not considering a merger of the two brands at this time.

However, any tie-up would probably trigger concerns about job losses given the significant levels of duplication in the rival companies’ distribution centres and head office operations.

It comes after Poundland was pulled back from the brink of collapse last year after failing to keep up with business rates payments to local councils across the country.

The bargain store enjoyed a boom during the recession but has fallen out of favour with shoppers in recent years amid complaints it was selling more items for more than £1.

US investor Gordon Brothers, which previously owned Laura Ashley, agreed to pump £80m into the company as part of the rescue deal with Pepco, Poundland’s Polish former parent company.

The bailout also resulted in around 200 store closures. Poundland now operates roughly 600 shops and employs 12,000 people across the UK.

Gordon Brothers, which also owns the LK Bennett and Radley fashion brands, has now launched a sale process for the chain.

That is despite insiders insisting that trading has improved and the business is now back in the black.

Advisers are aiming to wrap up a deal quickly to avoid any disruption to the retailer’s crucial Christmas trading period.

Poundstretcher, which operates more than 300 stores in the UK, was founded in 1981. It was snapped up by Fortress in 2024.

The discount retailer has been on an aggressive expansion drive in recent months, opening 12 new stores between June and August.

New York-based Fortress also owns the Bristol-based bar chain Loungers and last year invested $100m (£74m) in British chip designer Imagination.

Gordon Brothers, Fortress and Alvarez and Marsal declined to comment.

data.title: Ryanair boss refuses to apologise for ‘rapists’ remark
data.description:
Michael O’Leary, the Ryanair boss, has refused to apologise after comparing the discount airline’s rivals to rapists.

Mr O’Leary told journalists earlier this week that some travellers were “desperate to get to Ryanair’s low fares because they can’t afford to fly with the high-fare rapists around Europe”.

The Irish airline boss’s comment prompted a call from Rachel Morrogh, the head of the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre, for a “swift apology to survivors of rape and sexual violence”.

However, in a letter to Ms Morrogh, Mr O’Leary defended the comments and said he would not apologise.

The Ryanair chief said: “I was asked what I thought of rape, and answered that it was a heinous crime. I was also asked if describing high fare competitor airlines as high fare rapists somehow trivialised the crime of rape, and I was clear in my view that it did not.

“You are entirely free to hold a different opinion. But since I clearly did not trivialise the heinous crime of rape, I will certainly not be issuing any apology.”

Ms Morrogh said that Ireland’s National Rape Crisis Helpline, which the Dublin centre runs, had received calls from rape victims who were “upset and distressed” by Mr O’Leary’s comments.

She added: “We have enough work to be doing and survivors have enough trauma to face without lazy comments adding to it.

“I can’t imagine that you would ever use the term so flippantly again if you truly understood what it was like to survive rape.”

She claimed the Ryanair boss had deliberately used the phrase to gain attention, adding: “I wanted to let you know that you got the headline at a price rape survivors had to pay.”

Mr O’Leary said in his response that he would not be taking the centre up on an offer of free “training on sexual violence and the impact it has on people who have experienced it”.

He added that Ms Morrogh’s portrayal of his attitude to rape survivors was “both false and defamatory”.

Mr O’Leary’s comments came at Ryanair’s shareholder AGM, at which the airline boss said Ryanair would be “disputing” claims that part of a passenger’s body was sucked outside when a window on one of its aircraft broke while en route from Greece to Germany in July.

He also called for Martin Rolfe, the head of Britain’s air traffic control service, to be sacked after a computer meltdown that led to more than 2,000 flights being cancelled this week, branding him “incompetent” and an “overpaid failure”.

data.title: Britain is flogging off yet another beloved brand
data.description:
KitKats, created by Rowntree’s, are now made by Nestlé, of Switzerland. Cadbury’s Dairy Milk, and the rest of its brands, are now manufactured by Mondelēz International of the United States. Jaguar Land Rover is owned by India’s Tata, while even HP Sauce is now brought to your local greasy spoon cafe courtesy of Heinz Kraft.

We have long been used to some of the most beloved British brands being sold off to foreign conglomerates. Now it appears that Colman’s Mustard, and even Marmite, may join the list.

The Italians, the Americans and certainly the French would never allow their most valuable brands to be sold abroad in such a cavalier fashion. It is time Britain started protecting the few we have left, because very soon it will be too late.

There can be few more quintessentially English products than Colman’s. The fiery, tangy mustard goes perfectly with a full English breakfast, especially if your head is a little worse the wear after a heavy night, but it is hard to see it fitting any other kind of cuisine.

It emerged last week that Unilever is putting the brand up for sale as part of the clean-up of its sprawling empire. Bankers have been appointed to find a buyer for the brand as part of the wider deal to merge its food business with the American spice giant McCormick.

Apparently there is a risk of a “mustard monopoly”, given that it already owns the popular American brand French’s, although it is hard to believe regulators could really argue that Colman’s was really the same product as the insipid, tasteless yellow liquid created on the other side of the Atlantic. 

We will have to see what happens as the sale process gets under way. But whether it is a private equity firm or another food conglomerate the chances are that it will be sold abroad. Arguably Marmite will as well, given that McCormick will control the brand, although it will be majority owned by Unilever’s shareholders. Control of another celebrated brand will have left these shores.

There is no point in blaming Unilever for that. The company has been long overdue a radical overhaul after years of underperformance, when it seemed to care more about social activism than selling more soap or mayonnaise.

What happens to all the heritage wrapped up in the Colman’s brand? The mustard was created by Jeremiah Colman way back in the early 1800s, and by the 1820s it had become J & J Colman. From its Norwich base, it was one of the first great food brands of the industrial revolution, pioneering a model that was eventually copied all over the world.

Will all of that be preserved when one of the private equity firms gets its hands on it? Probably lots of promises will be made when the papers are signed, but they should be taken with a large pinch of salt (or mustard). Very few of those kinds of pledges are ever stuck to.

In reality, very few countries have been as happy as Britain has been to flog off their most valuable brands to anyone who feels like getting their chequebook out. Italy has its “golden powers regime” designed to protect assets of strategic national relevance. The United States has the Committee on Foreign Investment that can block deals, and there is little question the Trump White House would use it to stop the sale of Coca-Cola or Oreos.

And France of course, has laws to protect national assets, and in the past has used them to protect the yogurt manufacturer Danone from a foreign stake-holding. In most countries, the sale of a brand as historic as Colman’s would provoke a furious debate. Here in Britain we just let the investment bankers get on with hawking it around to the highest bidder.

That is not good enough. Sure, we all believe in a free market in corporate assets. But you hardly have to agree with Andy Burnham, with his student union tirades about “ending 40 years of neoliberalism” to wonder if the sell-off has not gone too far. After all, it is hard to see that any of the brands have been improved by their foreign owners.

Cadbury has lost much of the magic that once made it special. HP Sauce has, perhaps unsurprisingly, failed to conquer the world, while the less that is said about Jaguar Land Rover the better. If the foreign owner were taking all the heritage, and using it to build global mega-brands, with everyone from San Francisco to Shanghai queuing up for a bar of Dairy Milk, then it would be worthwhile. But it hasn’t happened.

Instead, ties with what were once their local communities have been weakened, and products have lost their identity. True, KitKats are still made in York, but Nestlé cut more than 400 jobs at the factory in April, while Cadbury’s closed its Bristol plant years ago. That might have happened under local management. But if we are being honest it would have been less likely.

It doesn’t have to work out like this. There is nothing wrong with Unilever selling Colman’s. But it would be perfectly possible for the Government to insist on a British buyer. There are plenty of food companies or UK based investors that might well be interested so long as the price was reasonable. In fact, there is one natural buyer.

Perhaps Unilever should be encouraged by ministers to sell it to Reckitt, the company that used to be known as Reckitt & Colman after it merged with J & J Colman in 1938. It is a well-managed business, with plenty of experience of running a portfolio of brands. And most of all, Colman’s would remain a British owned brand – which is exactly what it should be.

data.title: Britain to build turbines for Rolls-Royce mini-nuclear reactors
data.description:
British workers will build steam turbines for Rolls-Royce’s fleet of mini-nuclear reactors in a boost to domestic manufacturing.

Siemens Energy will produce the huge machines for a new generation of small modular reactors (SMRs) at its factory in Newcastle.

They will be used in the three Rolls-designed SMRs that are being built in Anglesey, as well as further reactors set to be built in the Czech Republic and Sweden.

It will be the first time large steam turbines have been made domestically in more than 20 years.

The expansion will follow an investment in the Newcastle factory understood to be worth tens of millions of pounds. It is expected to create 550 jobs.

It follows concerns raised by MPs that SMR components were set to be built abroad.

Rolls-Royce SMR said the decision by German engineering giant Siemens demonstrated how the company was “delivering its commitment to localisation, driving investment and re-shoring work that would have taken place overseas”.

Rolls-Royce SMR is an independent company, majority owned by Rolls-Royce but with investors including Qatar and France’s Perrodo family.

Chris Cholerton, the company’s chief executive, said: “We are building on a remarkable industrial legacy while creating and sustaining the skills and supply chain needed to deliver clean, secure and affordable energy for decades to come.”

Darren Davidson, of Siemens Energy, added: “We’re preparing to manufacture the next generation of steam turbines for small modular reactors, supporting energy security, creating skilled jobs and helping power the UK’s future energy mix.”

The Government awarded Rolls a contract to design and develop Britain’s first three SMRs last year.

They will be built in Anglesey, North Wales, in a project aimed at proving the commercial viability of the still-nascent technology by the mid-2030s. Each one will generate 470 megawatts of power.

Rolls selected Siemens Energy as its supplier of steam turbines last year, but there had been uncertainty about where the key components would be manufactured until now.

The British company faced a backlash earlier this year after it emerged that some other parts would be made overseas, including reactor pressure vessels that will be imported from either South Korea or the Czech Republic.

Labour ministers have set a target for 70pc of components to be made in Britain, and on Thursday they hailed the announcement by Siemens as proof their plan to “reindustrialise Britain” was working.

Miatta Fahnbulleh, the Energy Secretary, said: “Producing these components here in the UK will help strengthen our energy security, reduce our exposure to volatile international gas markets, create new export opportunities for British industry, and reindustrialise the UK.”

Jonathan Reynolds, the Business Secretary, added: “Building small modular reactors here in the UK presents huge benefits for us, from more export opportunities to more jobs on the ground at home.”

The Newcastle factory is expected to make both high-pressure turbines and valve casings.

It will also become the service hub for the turbines in the Rolls SMR fleet, ensuring a pipeline of work for the site that is expected to last decades.

The historic Parsons Works is the site once run by Sir Charles Parsons, the revered British engineer who helped to revolutionise marine propulsion with his invention of the multi-stage steam turbine.

It was established in 1889 and was where the steam turbine for Calder Hall – the world’s first commercial nuclear power station, in Cumbria – was built.

Grid-scale steam turbines have not been manufactured in the UK since the early 2000s, when Siemens scaled back its operations in Newcastle.

A steam turbine for a nuclear power plant has not been built in Britain since the early 1990s when one was supplied for the Sizewell B plant in Suffolk.

Tom Greatrex, of the Nuclear Industry Association, said: “This is what reindustrialisation looks like: a vital clean energy project reviving our old manufacturing capabilities to provide good, skilled jobs where we need them.

“The announcement is a real vote of confidence in industrial Britain and shows what SMRs and nuclear projects can deliver for this country.”

data.title: Reform drums up business support at conference
data.description:
Large firms are flocking to Reform UK’s national conference as the party prepares to host its inaugural business day.

First Bus, BT, Vodafone, Google, Heathrow, JCB, Dubai Ports and TikTok are among the businesses sponsoring or running events at the three-day summit which starts on Thursday in Birmingham.

The party’s decision to host a business day forms part of a wider Reform UK strategy to replace the Conservatives as the main opposition party to Andy Burnham’s government by fighting Labour on economic grounds.

In recent weeks, the party has unveiled plans for the biggest welfare shake-up “in a generation” by scrapping key benefits to save £50bn a year, more than double what the Tories plan to save, as well as pledging a £30 rebate for taxpayers stuck on hold to His Majesty’s Revenue and Customs (HMRC).

To appeal to wealthy backers, they are also offering conference packages worth up to £3,000, which include a champagne breakfast with Nigel Farage, an opportunity to meet and network with senior Reform leaders and a three-course meal in the Platinum hospitality area.

‘Increased engagement’

The party has toned down its offerings from last year in an attempt to professionalise, scrapping offers of custom cocktail naming rights and the delivery of bottles of sparkling wine to business stands.

A Reform UK spokesman told The Telegraph: “Engagement from British business has increased significantly. Companies across the country recognise they need to understand Reform and what a future Reform government could mean for them.

“Businesses now realise that the possibility of a Reform government is very real and are acting accordingly.”

Until 2025, Reform had a relatively low attendance from big business compared with similar events organised by Labour and the Tories.

But the influx of big business to this year’s annual event signals that the corporate world is taking the possibility of a Reform government seriously, as the party continues to outperform rivals in voter intention polling.

Crypto sidelined

Reform, which topped polls for almost 16 consecutive months between March 2025 and July 2026 and won hundreds of councillors in May, is now in second place trailing the Labour Party following a so-called Burnham bounce.

Meanwhile, Mr Farage is also believed to be sidelining crypto companies in favour of mainstream corporates following a backlash over the Reform leader’s £5m gift from Christopher Harborne, the Bitcoin billionaire.

Crypto companies are not among the businesses sponsoring the 2026 conference, which last year included donations from crypto payments firm Zebec.

The party has also scrapped perks it had previously offered to crypto industry leaders, including free tickets and access to senior figures, according to City AM, in a notable departure from previous years.

Conferences and the sponsorship fees that come in from big businesses are one of the ways that political parties raise revenue for their campaigning efforts.

A Heathrow spokesman said the airport had “a long history of constructive engagement across the political spectrum”.

He said: “Like many businesses – from airlines to pubs and banks to supermarkets – it is common practice to sponsor events at party conferences to engage policymakers and ensure they better understand the needs of consumers and the economy.”

data.title: Paying for speed: 5G ‘fast lanes’ risk steeper phone bills
data.description:
Speaking on the sidelines of Thruxton’s motor circuit in Hampshire on a soggy September afternoon, Max Taylor felt inspired.

“The UK needs to go faster,” the VodafoneThree boss said as he unveiled a new premium 5G service. “It’s what customers want, it’s what they’re asking us for – but it’s also what they’re going to need in the future.”

Vodafone’s new and improved 5G service will be a boon for Britons who have long struggled with scratchy calls and buffering videos.

This is just one frontier in a new era for the internet.

Alongside rivals Virgin Media O2 and BT-owned EE, Vodafone is calling for a watering down of crucial laws to help unleash faster 5G signals.

These reforms could open up a raft of new opportunities, the companies argue, from easing network congestion at concerts and sports events to allowing customers to prioritise urgent calls or online activities.

For consumers, however, access to these 5G fast lanes will probably come at a cost.

Slow and patchy mobile coverage is a reality of everyday life in Britain, which has download speeds so poor that they rank below countries including Kazakhstan and Cambodia.

Industry bosses and analysts point to a number of causes, including cumbersome planning laws and razor-thin margins that have stifled investment by network operators.

As 5G upgrades provide ever greater network capacity, there are now glimpses of improvement.

SuperMobile, Vodafone’s premium service, promises speeds up to four times faster than regular 5G.

EE has also launched its own fast-lane service, which offers speedier connections at crowded locations such as Wembley Stadium.

These innovations take advantage of 5G technology known as “slicing”, which allows different parts of a mobile network to be used for different purposes.

The changes come after Ofcom in 2023 revised its rules on net neutrality to clarify that mobile and broadband operators can offer premium services.

It was a modest revision of a decades-old principle dictating that all internet traffic and data must be treated equally.

Tearing through restrictions

Now, mobile network operators want to go further and tear up restrictions that prevent individual apps and services from being prioritised.

This could mean, for example, that a reveller trying to hail an Uber when leaving a busy venue would be prioritised over someone uploading videos of their night out to Instagram.

Equally, someone trying to connect to an electric-car charger in a multi-storey car park could be fast-tracked, while users could choose to prioritise an important video call over other activities.

For businesses, too, there are benefits. For example, a food stall operator could secure priority to process card payments or a ticketing company could secure extra bandwidth before an expected rush of sales.

BT, Virgin Media O2 and Vodafone are all lobbying ministers to allow these changes as part of the ongoing mobile market review.

“Outdated net neutrality rules mean that customers aren’t realising the full benefits of our investment,” says Jeanie York, VVMO2’s chief technology officer.

“Reforming these rules should be a priority for the Government, enabling operators to be more efficient in managing traffic and to use the full capabilities of the latest technology.”

A BT spokesman said: “The Mobile Market Review is an opportunity to modernise the regulatory and policy framework governing mobile networks, which was developed for a very different era of the internet almost 20 years ago.

“A more flexible approach to network management and innovation would help deliver better connectivity, support new technologies and encourage continued investment in world-class infrastructure for the UK.”

Critics warn that any move to discriminate between different types of data risks creating a “two-tier” internet where network operators control who sees what. This, they argue, could ultimately have implications for freedom of expression.

Perhaps most concerningly for consumers, these upgrades will come at a cost. Vodafone SuperMobile will cost contract customers an extra £3 a month, while EE’s upgraded service will be an extra £5.

However, there are concerns that Mr Healey may raise levies on banks in his Budget on Oct 28.

Mr Burnham dropped into a meeting between Mr Dimon and Varun Chandra, the Prime Minister’s chief business adviser, according to the Financial Times.

Mr Dimon has previously warned Andy Burnham against the idea. The JP Morgan boss said in an interview earlier this year that there would be “adverse consequences” if Labour targeted lenders with fresh windfall taxes.

He said: “It would be one more negative on that bucket of things you got to think about.

“I always thought it was wrong. We’re a great citizen [in the UK]. We hire people there. We want to be bigger there. We train people there. We hire veterans there.”

The American banker added: “So if a government decides to do it, there’s nothing I can do, but it will over time cause decisions made that they may not like.”

There have been growing calls from unions and campaigners to raise taxes on banks.

Paul Nowak, the general secretary of the Trades Union Congress, has argued that Mr Burnham could raise £9bn in four years simply by reversing the previous Conservative government’s cut to the bank surcharge. The group has argued that this could be used to fund cuts to energy bills.

She said during a visit to London last month that “money moves with its feet”, pointing out that “even Frankfurt and Paris are lower” when it comes to taxes for banks.

Mr Healey said this week that “doubling down” on “more growth generated in more places” will be a central priority of his first Budget.

He has refused to rule out raising taxes, but promised to “balance the books” and “control public spending”.

data.title: Johnson & Johnson offers £4.1bn to settle talcum powder cancer claims
data.description:
Johnson & Johnson (J&J) has agreed to pay an estimated $5.5bn (£4.1bn) to resolve tens of thousands of claims that its baby powder caused ovarian cancer.

The pharmaceutical giant’s offer of a settlement could end a decade-long legal battle that has dogged the company.

Erik Haas, vice-president of litigation at J&J, said the claims that its talcum powder products caused cancer were “meritless” ‌but said the company was willing ⁠to settle to get closure.

The settlement covers around 76,000 claims and must be accepted by 95pc of the ovarian cancer claimants in state or federal court before it becomes final.

J&J previously settled the majority of cases alleging that its talc contained asbestos and caused mesothelioma, a rare but aggressive cancer affected the lungs, abdomen or heart.

Mr Haas said: “While we are confident the company would have ultimately prevailed with further litigation, as it has in the vast majority of cases tried to date, this resolution allows the company to put this matter behind it and remain focused on its mission to develop medicines and devices that save ⁠lives.”

J&J expects to pay $3bn in 2027, and it will make further payments in 2028.

More than 3,000 people filed lawsuits at Britain’s High Court last year alleging that either they or a family member developed ovarian cancer or mesothelioma as a result of using Johnson’s Baby Powder between 1965 and 2023.

The settlements announced on Monday included groups who filed claims in federal and state courts.

J&J ended global sales of baby powder containing the mineral talc in 2023, switching to a formulation based on corn starch.

The settlements come after cases were put on hold for more than three years after a series of bankruptcy filings by J&J.

It filed three bankruptcies through a shell-company subsidiary in an ‌effort to settle the cases. Each bankruptcy ended in dismissal and the litigation resumed in March 2025.

Chris Seeger, an attorney who represents about 2,500 clients with talc claims and helped negotiate the agreement, said J&J could ultimately pay $7bn or more.

The settlement assigns specific values to qualifying ovarian cancer claims but does not cap J&J’s total payout.

He said: “We got ‌a fair settlement, and our clients are going to be happy with it.”

data.title: Burnham to cut energy bills by up to £200 for benefits claimants
data.description:
Andy Burnham is to cut up to £200 off benefits claimants’ energy bills this winter as the Iran war sends gas and fuel prices surging.

The Prime Minister is exploring providing targeted subsidies to millions of households living in fuel poverty including those who do not currently qualify for existing support.

Whitehall officials are understood to have started drawing up the scheme after the outbreak of the US-Iran war put a squeeze on global oil and gas supplies coming out of the Strait of Hormuz trade choke point.

The energy price cap is poised to jump from £1,663 to £1,723 in October, with analysts forecasting that it will rise again to £1,872 in January – a total increase of about £200 across the winter.

The support scheme, called the Energy Price Protection Payment (EPPP), is “ready” to be implemented in January, according to industry insiders. It would aim to mitigate some or all of the impact of the rise in energy prices.

It could be announced as soon as the Budget on Oct 28, or potentially in late November when the next energy price cap adjustment is confirmed.

There are also discussions about whether a wider package of support could be provided to all households but this would be more expensive and could clash with the vow by John Healey, the Chancellor, to protect the public finances.

No final decision has been made yet on whether to proceed with the EPPP or how much the support will be worth.

It would apply to people who already receive the Warm Homes Discount as well as some others deemed in need of support.

To receive the discount, a claimant must be in receipt of benefits. But sources said the support was poorly targeted and did not cover another estimated 2.5 million extra households who were still classed as being in fuel poverty.

It is unclear whether the EPPP would seek to target only some or all of those households.

One person familiar with the plan said it could be part of a wider energy bills intervention that could “layer” support to benefits claimants on top of more universal measures.

However, they stressed the final shape of any package would be determined by the strength of the public finances and how energy prices evolve.

The Iran crisis has sent European gas prices to their highest point since 2022, prompting fresh concerns about the cost of living at a time when Mr Burnham has pledged to put “more money in people’s pockets”.

He has already cut VAT to zero on electricity bills, saving a typical household about £45 per year.

However, the cut has already been wiped out by rising energy costs and is scheduled to expire at the end of March.

Industry sources suggested that the Government was looking at other ways to bring down bills in the long term such as reducing or eliminating network charges and green levies.

Ministers cut bills by £150 for households last year by removing the energy company obligation and 75pc of the renewable obligation in the last Budget.

However, a letter on Friday from more than 120 businesses, trade groups and charities including Nationwide, Octopus Energy and British Gas urged Labour to go further and cut levies by an additional £100 a year.

They said: “Moving electricity levies from both business and household bills to government spending would immediately make energy costs more affordable and competitive, providing a greatly needed boost for our manufacturing industries and tackling cost of living challenges.”

Miatta Fahnbulleh, the Energy Secretary, is also thought to be championing proposals inside the Government for a so-called block tariff. This would grant all households a discounted “block” of electricity and gas, with anything used above that threshold charged at the normal rate.

A government spokesman said: “The Chancellor is fully focused on giving families and businesses breathing space and helping ease cost pressures.”

data.title: Jaguar Land Rover to axe 4,000 jobs
data.description:
Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) has confirmed plans to cut 4,000 jobs as its battles against competition from low-cost Chinese rivals and the shift to electric vehicles.

The company said on Monday that it would make the cuts over the next two years amid “intense competition and ongoing geopolitical uncertainty”.

Bosses insisted the move was necessary “to build a stronger, more competitive JLR”, as they targeted £1.7bn of savings from a wider overhaul of the business.

PB Balaji, the carmaker’s chief executive, added: “We recognise this will be difficult news for colleagues affected, and are committed to supporting everyone with care, fairness and respect.”

The cuts represent a major setback to Andy Burnham’s pledge to reindustrialise Britain.

It is understood they will largely fall on white-collar, salaried workers across JLR’s UK business and will not affect employees working in car production.

Some staff working in the manufacturer’s overseas divisions are also expected to be given the opportunity to take voluntary redundancy, which could reduce the effect on the British business.

Around 30,000 of the company’s 44,000 employees are based in the UK.

JLR’s global headquarters are in Coventry, while it operates major factories in manufacturing sites in Solihull, Wolverhampton and Merseyside.

No state bailout

MPs have warned that the cuts will have a “devastating” effect, with Mr Balaji set to hold a meeting with ministers and union officials on Tuesday.

He will sit down with Sharon Graham, the general secretary of Unite the Union, and Jonathan Reynolds, the Business Secretary, who has already made clear that there will be no money for a bailout of the company to protect jobs.

However, Mr Reynolds appeared to leave the door open for the Government to offer other forms of support.

“If it’s about long-term investment in the future, we do invest alongside industry on that,” he told Laura Kuenssberg’s Sunday morning BBC TV show.

At Tuesday’s meeting, Mr Balaji is expected to bring up the Government’s electric vehicle mandate – which could be watered down under changes being considered by ministers – as well as general pressures on the business, such as high energy costs and taxes on employment.

However, a source close to the company acknowledged that although improving conditions in the UK would help, JLR’s troubles were global in nature and echoed those of European giants, such as Volkswagen and Stellantis.

JLR, owned by Indian conglomerate Tata, is under pressure to shore up its finances amid rising costs and a slump in sales.

Revenues fell by almost 10pc in the first quarter, while pre-tax profits dropped by two thirds to £109m.

The carmaker, whose largest market is North America, has been rocked by Donald Trump’s 10pc tariff on vehicle imports to the US.

It is also still reeling from a crippling cyber attack that shut down production for more than a month and is estimated to have cost the company £1.9bn.

Further supply chain disruption and tough competition from cut-price Chinese rivals have also taken a toll.

Mr Balaji said the company was investing at least £15bn in electrification overall while it also seeks to make £1.7bn of savings.

Union officials are pushing for those who are losing their jobs to be retrained, potentially with support from the Government.

Unite’s Ms Graham said: “While the cuts planned are not expected to impact the UK manufacturing footprint, we need to ensure that the company is doing all it can to avoid unnecessary job losses amongst its highly skilled white collar workers.

“JLR’s vague statement today was not helpful and has only created increased uncertainty.

“Once again Unite will leave no stone unturned to support JLR workers. It cannot be acceptable that workers again are made to pay the price.”

She added that the union supported changes to the zero-emission vehicle mandate, which along with high energy costs had been “crippling the industry”.

A spokesman for Andy Burnham said on Monday that the Government remained “in close contact” with JLR.

They added: “We understand that this will be an uncertain and concerning time for affected workers, their families and the wider communities.”
