data.title: Net zero grid upgrades drive a £200bn energy industry civil war
data.description:
The subsea cable known as Eastern Green Link 1 will slip into the water at Torness, east of Edinburgh, before resurfacing near the coastal town of Seaham, County Durham.

It is often referred to as a “bootstrap” by energy insiders. But that doesn’t do the project’s scale justice.

Developers say that by 2029 the 120-mile electricity “superhighway” will help unlock Scotland’s renewable energy reserves by transporting enough power for two million homes southward.

At an estimated cost of £2.5bn, it is probably one of the most expensive infrastructure schemes you’ve never heard of – perhaps because it lacks the visibility of a railway, road or bridge.

Yet amid severe delays and escalating costs, Eastern Green Link 1 and schemes like it are now beginning to attract more attention.

The cable and its sister project, Eastern Green Link 2, were originally meant to cost a combined £3.4bn, a figure that has since doubled to an estimated £6.8bn.

Elsewhere, some grid-improvement schemes have already seen their projected budgets balloon by nearly 500pc.

Against the backdrop of a wider £200bn upgrade under way across Britain’s power network, critics fear that it risks becoming a fresh HS2-style fiasco for the Government, with millions of households and businesses left to pick up the tab.

“This is going to make HS2 look like a slick, well-executed operation,” one worried energy industry source says.

Sam Richards, the chief executive of Britain Remade, a clean energy pressure group, adds: “The simple truth is that Britain is building too much grid, at too high a price.”

Squeeze on household bills

Britain’s power grid is an engineering marvel. It spans 530,000 miles of cables, including some 10,000 miles of high-voltage transmission lines – the motorways of the system – and another 520,000 miles of lower-voltage distribution networks that carry power to people’s homes.

It was largely built through the 1950s, ’60s and ’70s and designed to manage power for a highly centralised system that depended on a relatively small number of coal-fired and nuclear power stations.

But to reach net zero carbon emissions, significant changes are required.

In a system dominated by renewable-energy generators, such as wind and solar farms, the network will instead rely on a large number of smaller power plants scattered across the country.

Along with a need to modernise infrastructure, the “great grid upgrade” set in train under successive Labour and Conservative governments is driven largely by net zero.

In total, it is expected to trigger more than £200bn of investment across distribution, transmission and interconnectors between this year and 2040, according to consultancy Baringa.

This includes £68bn alone to expand the UK’s transmission grid, the high-voltage cables that carry power over long distances to cities.

Households and businesses ultimately pay for all this work through their energy bills, which are rising to fund it.

According to tracker website Electricitybills.uk, the network component of a typical household’s bill is on course to have risen by 65pc, or from £207 to £342 per year, between 2025 and 2030.

Contrary to the oft-repeated mantra of Labour ministers, this means network charges, rather than volatile gas prices, are currently the biggest driver of domestic bill increases.

At the same time, modelling by SQE Energy suggests most industrial and commercial businesses face increases of between 60pc and 90pc in transmission network charges over the next few years.

“If you put it all together, including new expenditure and what you have to spend on ‘catch-up’ refurbishment of assets that should really have taken place previously, it’s a huge number – probably our biggest infrastructure undertaking as a country at the moment,” says Nick Forrest, a partner at Baringa.

Yet despite the vast scale of spending – and the outsized impact it is having on bills – energy suppliers including EDF and Octopus Energy say the grid upgrade programme has been rammed through with little scrutiny or regard to the costs it will impose on their customers.

One reason they are concerned is that polling shows consumers will probably blame them – rather than grid companies – for the ever-growing bills landing on their doormats.

But like HS2, there are also concerns about complicated regulatory processes.

“It’s f------ impenetrable,” complains one executive at a major energy company.

“You have to live and breathe this stuff to really understand it. We weren’t happy with the way it was pushed through.”

Another insider described it as “opaque and undemocratic”.

And what is now ringing further alarm bells is a string of delays and cost increases that threaten to push the cost of the grid-upgrade programme even higher.

Along with the Eastern Green Link cable schemes, several major projects are reporting surging cost inflation.

For example, a report quietly published by Ofgem in May revealed that a string of eight projects being built in Scotland by SSE were forecasting total cost increases of 284pc on average.

This included a staggering 467pc projected cost increase for work to upgrade transmission lines between Loch Buidhe and Spittal.

Ofgem has not disclosed the potential cost of the overruns in cash terms, or what their impact could be on bills.

But the available figures are not encouraging.

Another one of the eight projects is a high-voltage subsea cable between Spittal and Peterhead.

The exact cost of this individual link remains guarded, but SSE recently awarded a mammoth €2bn (£1.7bn) combined contract to Danish manufacturer NKT to supply cables for both the Spittal-Peterhead route and a separate Western Isles link.

Ofgem analysis reveals the Spittal-Peterhead scheme’s estimated overall budget has increased by 111pc since initial projections.

This has led to the watchdog allowing SSE to spend more on early construction costs, but it is still deciding whether any further increases are reasonable.

Crippling production bottlenecks

The regulator has said it will “rigorously challenge” all cost rises, but its past record is weak and experts fear it will have little grounds to challenge companies for higher spending that is being driven by external factors.

“There are lots of factors in the control of the transmission and distribution companies, but there are also quite a lot of things outside of their control, from the time it takes to get planning approvals to global supply chains,” says Baringa’s Forrest.

For example, Ofgem announced in 2022 that the Eastern Green Link 1 and 2 projects would cost a combined £3.4bn.

But when the developers of the scheme went to the market to secure the materials and services they needed, they found the costs were far higher than expected.

Ofgem was reluctantly approving a budget of £4.3bn alone by 2024 for Eastern Green Link 2 – after managing to find just £67m of spending it deemed unnecessary.

The surging costs have been blamed on the global rush towards renewables, which has sent prices for grid equipment surging as countries around the world all try to buy the same things at once.

According to the International Energy Agency, the cost of cables and transformers surged 91pc and 72pc higher between 2019 and 2024, with manufacturers also taking longer to deliver as they battle production bottlenecks.

Any kind of delay is a nightmare for developers, because it forces them to pay contractors for longer or spend more on storing equipment until it is needed.

But understanding exactly what is driving costs can be difficult because of a paucity of publicly available information, says Ed Hezlet, an energy expert at Onward, a Right-leaning think tank.

In many cases, National Grid and other companies are allowed to keep the finances of individual schemes hidden because they are deemed “commercially sensitive”.

“There’s evidence that costs have shifted up very significantly since 2022, but it’s hard to really know what’s going on,” Hezlet says.

“That’s worrying, because if you take the HS2 analogy, you definitely want to find out if something’s massively running over budget early rather than later – so you can actually talk about it properly and address it.

“Ultimately, billpayers are going to be footing the bill for all of this. So there should be far more transparency about both the cost and the progress of these projects.”

‘Limited amount of information’

EDF, one of Britain’s biggest energy suppliers, has also warned that there is currently a lack of transparency about both the scale and cause of the cost increases, not all of which can be pinned on inflation alone.

The company claims it is “impossible” to fully assess how bad things are based on “the limited amount of information available”, but adds: “There has been substantial supply chain cost inflation over the past few years, and this is likely to continue as countries across the globe tackle the same electricity network and generation challenges.

“We estimate costs have risen two or three times since initial transmission operator forecasts. This is corroborated by our own experience of connection cost increases for our generation projects.”

At the same time, it says, generators seeking to connect to the grid are facing average delays of two years – meaning the extensive upgrade work being undertaken may not actually be needed as quickly as thought.

Taken together, EDF and others argue this should prompt a rethink about whether the money being spent on grid projects is still good value.

“If we want to change direction, now is the last moment where this is possible without creating significant sunk costs, or delaying projects that are much-needed within the system,” EDF added.

In response, the Energy Networks Association lobby group insists the upgrade will deliver value for money.

In fact, Lawrence Slade, the group’s chief executive, says: “Network investment is supporting the connection of more affordable and reliable homegrown energy – it is an ongoing process that is creating thousands of jobs today, strengthening our long-term energy independence and ensuring customers will save on their bills in the future.

“Ofgem has stated that transmission network investment is expected to lead to around £80 of savings for bill payers by 2031 compared to not investing, which means bills are expected to be around £30 lower than they would have been had investment not been made.”

An Ofgem spokesman added: “While upgrades will requires upfront investment, failing to invest would also increase costs for consumers through higher constraint and balancing payments caused by grid bottlenecks.”

But just how far behind is Britain’s “great grid upgrade”?

Some of the best clues come from documents published by the National Energy System Operator (Neso), which is tasked with managing the grid day-to-day.

Of some 90 projects deemed essential for Labour’s clean power target, 64 have delivery dates falling after the all-important year 2030.

Among them is Eastern Green Link 2, which Neso says is needed by 2029. Instead, it is not on course to connect until December 2035.

Similarly the Beauly-Denny upgrade in the Highlands is needed by 2029 on Neso’s own numbers, but has substation works attached to it dated as late as November 2036.

The Telegraph sent questions to the Government, Neso, grid companies and trade bodies at the heart of the grid upgrade asking about the surging delays, cost overruns and the effect on bills. All refused to give detailed answers.

Kayte O’Neill, the chief operating officer at Neso, insisted that documents published by the quango did not represent a “Clean Power 2030 delivery tracker”.

However, she admits that delivering a decarbonised grid by 2030, the political target demanded by Labour in 2024, is proving challenging.

“Neso has consistently advised that delivering clean power by 2030 is a significant challenge,” she says.

“Achieving it will require cross-sector collaboration, including accelerated delivery of critical network infrastructure from transmission owners, implementation of connections reform and continued coordination between industry, government and Ofgem.”

A spokesman for the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero said: “We are reversing decades of underinvestment in the grid, alongside the private sector, to build an energy system that can bring down bills for good.”

Chris Bowden, the chief executive of SQE Energy, a supplier that manages grid connections for businesses, says the cost overruns and delays were already showing up in the data.

He argues that the cost of reaching Labour’s target in just four years will be huge – especially for industry and business, which are largely unprotected from price rises.

Bowden says: “On bills, the domestic impact gets most of the attention, but the industrial and commercial side is larger and less discussed.

“Our modelling suggests most industrial and commercial businesses face increases of 60-90pc in transmission network charges over the next few years.”

The chief executive adds: “One client’s charges are set to more than double to over £17m by 2029.”

With such substantial cost increases coming down the pipeline, some critics now argue that the Government should press pause on major grid spending until it can be sure everything planned is needed.

For example, Greg Jackson, the boss of Octopus Energy, Britain’s biggest energy supplier, has argued that new technologies, such as AI and dynamic line rating, which can help to squeeze more capacity out of existing power lines, should be exploited fully before consumers are tapped for costly upgrades.

He has also argued that major market reforms, such as switching from Britain’s current national electricity pricing system to a series of smaller, more localised markets, could remove the need for such massive works by forcing energy companies to be more efficient.

This is because energy producers will be encouraged to build out power suppliers in different parts of the country to support local markets, removing the need to transport energy from north to south.

In an interview with The Telegraph this year, Jackson suggested that this change could invalidate tens of billions of pounds currently set to be spent on grid upgrades.

A report produced this year for Octopus by FTI Consulting, a lobbying group, suggested that moving to locational pricing would render between £22bn and £30bn of planned transmission upgrades unnecessary.

This would potentially unlock between £55bn and £73bn in consumer bill savings between 2030 and 2050, it said.

Richards, at Britain Remade, agrees. “The way to reduce the amount of grid infrastructure that’s needed is by switching to local pricing.

“By cutting bills where the power is generated, more will get used at source, cutting the amount of wires and pylons needed.

“On top of this, planning delays, vexatious legal challenges and excessive regulation on new energy infrastructure is driving up grid build costs.

“Continuing to reform the planning system is essential if the Government is to deliver on its pledge to reduce energy bills.”

Doing so, he argues, will be essential if Andy Burnham, the Prime Minister, is also to meet his promise to put more money into voters’ pockets.

Onward’s Hezlet also fears that failing to reappraise grid costs now could have painful and long-lasting consequences.

“There’s good reason to be concerned because this stuff is basically going to be locked into our bills for 45 years,” he says.

Chris O’Shea, the boss of British Gas owner Centrica, is also concerned.

He argues that Burnham should consider moving more of the grid upgrade costs off bills and into general taxation – a prospect that may have little appeal as John Healey, the Chancellor, grapples with existing black holes in his Budget.

“Upgrading Britain’s energy networks is essential if we’re going to build the low-carbon, secure energy system the country needs,” O’Shea says. “But we must be honest about how that investment is paid for.”

The boss of British Gas adds: “Loading too much of the cost onto bills risks putting more pressure on households and making life harder for businesses, particularly smaller firms that are the backbone of the economy and already facing tough conditions.

“Major infrastructure investment is best funded through general taxation, which is fairer, more transparent and better reflects the national importance of these upgrades.”

So far, however, ministers have proved reluctant to back down on their grid spending splurge.

Miatta Fahnbulleh, the Energy Secretary, said in a recent radio interview with LBC that the upgrade work was a necessity.

“I don’t think, if we did not invest in the infrastructure of our energy system, anyone would forgive us,” she said.

“It is not a choice to make sure that we are upgrading our energy system. We absolutely need to do that.”

As bills surge, households are unlikely to forgive Labour for the alternative either.

data.title: Global coal demand hits record high as Iran war cuts gas supplies
data.description:
Global coal consumption is set to hit a new record this year as war in the Middle East drives up global gas prices.

The International Energy Agency (IEA) said coal use would rise 1.2pc to a record 8.94 billion tonnes, after previously predicting that demand for the fossil fuel would decline.

The Paris-based agency said high gas prices and demand for air-conditioning, driven by the climate effect of the El Niño weather phenomenon, were pushing up coal consumption.

It linked the surge to the ongoing Iran war.

The agency said: “Although virtually no coal shipments pass through the Strait of Hormuz, the disruption has nonetheless affected coal markets by pushing up natural gas prices due to the plunge in liquefied natural gas shipments through the Strait.

“This has in turn encouraged more coal-fired generation in countries with gas-fired power fleets and spare coal capacity.”

The IEA predicted global demand for coal will “rise above previous expectations amid higher demand from import-dependent countries, such as Japan and Korea”, after global gas prices soared.

It added that this year’s so-called “Godzilla” El Niño weather pattern would lead to more coal demand from countries in Asia, such as India and Vietnam, as high temperatures lead to more demand for air-conditioning and lower hydropower output.

Coal use has been in long-term decline in Western economies as they switch to gas and renewables. However, usage has remained high in many developing economies and China, while Mr Trump has sought to encourage more coal production in the US.

A kilowatt-hour of power generated by burning coal typically releases a kilogram of CO2 – double that of gas. A typical UK household consumes 12,000 kilowatt-hours of energy a year.

The rise in coal use coincides with scientific reports that August was the world’s joint hottest month on record, with global temperatures at 1.65C above pre-industrial times.

Last month was the hottest August on record, with Western Europe experiencing its warmest ever summer, scientists from the EU’s Copernicus Climate Change Service said.

A run of heatwaves from May to August caused droughts in the UK, France, Hungary, Romania and Serbia, with major rivers, such as the Rhine and Danube, seeing exceptionally low flows.

Prof Friederike Otto, who specialises in climate science at Imperial College London, said: “You don’t need to be a climate scientist to see the evidence of climate change; you just need to look out of your window.

“Until we stop burning coal, oil and gas, these record-shattering months will simply keep on coming.”

The IEA said coal demand could increase again next year if the Strait of Hormuz remains closed.

data.title: 160-year-old Devon ‘war metal’ mine to reopen
data.description:
A century-old tungsten mine in Devon is set to restart production after receiving £71m in taxpayer funding.

In the latest effort to boost Britain’s rearmament, the Government’s National Wealth Fund (NWF) has invested in Tungsten West, the owner of Hemerdon mine near Plymouth.

The cash will be used to reopen Hemerdon for the first time in eight years, with the mine boasting some of the largest tungsten reserves in the world.

As part of the deal, the NWF will take a 7pc stake in Tungsten West for £36m before lending the business £35m.

It reflects a drive to make the UK more self-sufficient in critical minerals, particularly metals vital to defence.

Recent conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East have sent demand for tungsten surging, which is one of the most dense and heavy metals.

It is used in everything from hypersonic missile nose cones to armour-piercing bullets, bunker-busting bombs and “airburst” counter-drone shells.

John Healey, the new Chancellor, said: “We are living in a more dangerous world, which is why backing British industry is more important than ever before.

“That is what this deal does. We are tapping into one of the largest deposits of tungsten in the world, right here in the UK.”

The Hemerdon mine was first discovered in 1867 and mined during both world wars before closing in 1944.

It was briefly reopened between 2015 and 2018 before shutting again because of a lack of funds.

‘Increasing global demand’

Tungsten West, which is listed on London’s alternative investment market, was founded in 2019 with the aim of reopening the mine, which contains the fourth-largest tungsten reserves in the world.

Oliver Holbourn, the chief of the NWF, said: “There is strong and increasing global demand for tungsten, supported by its strategic applications in defence, next generation energy and aerospace.

“In Hemerdon, the UK has one of the largest deposits of tungsten in the world right on our doorstep.”

Tungsten West is set to start mining tin and tungsten at the Hemerdon mine by the end of this year before returning to full production in early 2027.

China produces roughly 80pc of the world’s tungsten supplies. However, prices of the critical metal have surged in the past year as a result of export restrictions imposed by Beijing.

Britain imports the entirety of its tungsten supplies from countries including France, Germany and China.

However, at full production the Hemerdon mine is expected to produce 3,300 tonnes of tungsten concentrate a year – equivalent to 20pc of world supplies outside China.

Jeff Court, Tungsten West’s chief executive, said: “Hemerdon is a world-class, low-cost and long-life tungsten and tin resource in the UK.

“It is extremely important to us that we prioritise UK requirements for this critical metal to support domestic demand, including strategic initiatives across defence and next generation energy.”

data.title: FTSE aerospace supplier sold to US bidder for £1.9bn
data.description:
A 103-year-old UK aerospace supplier is poised to leave the London stock market after being sold to a US private equity firm.

Bodycote, which is one of the world’s leading metallurgy companies, is to be taken over by New York’s Veritas Capital for £1.85bn.

It will see the Macclesfield company enter private hands for the first time in more than half a century, following its initial stock market listing in 1972.

Bodycote’s takeover is one of a trio of deals announced on Tuesday that will reignite concerns about the ailing health of the London stock market.

Gamma Communications, a FTSE 250 telecoms company, separately agreed a £1.1bn sale to Epris, a London private equity firm. Capricorn Energy, a Scottish oil-and-gas company, struck a deal to sell itself to Norway’s oldest oil company, DNO, for £292m.

Bodycote is the world’s biggest provider of specialist metallurgical treatments, spanning a global network of around 135 workshops.

The FTSE 250 company was started as a textiles manufacturer in Leicestershire in 1923 before moving into the metallurgy industry in the 1970s.

The metals it makes are used in everything from Rolls-Royce’s aerospace engines to specialist drills for undersea mines. It has around 4,000 employees.

The takeover will see Bodycote’s shareholders paid 940p per share, marking a 44pc premium on its closing price on July 7, the day before Veritas submitted its initial offer.

James Dimitri, from Veritas, said: “Bodycote has established itself as a global leader in providing essential technologies for performance metallurgy across a range of mission-critical end markets.”

Veritas is an American private equity firm with around $42bn (£36bn) worth of investments.

Since its launch, Veritas has made more than 145 acquisitions of mostly British and American businesses, including Scottish energy consultancy Wood Mackenzie in 2023.

London’s shrinking stock market

The takeover is the latest in a series of acquisitions that have seen some of Britain’s biggest companies pulled off the London Stock Exchange.

Capricorn Energy, which also announced a deal to go private on Tuesday, owns stakes in four oil and gas fields in the Egyptian desert, and is exploring more sites in the area.

DNO, which was started in 1971, is listed on the Oslo Stock Exchange and has oil sites in the Middle East, West Africa and the North Sea.

Berkshire-based Gamma sells phone and internet services to businesses across Western Europe, including the University of Derby and the AA.

Low valuations have made London-listed companies attractive to international buyers. It has fuelled an exodus from the London Stock Exchange, with the number of listed companies falling from 2,365 a decade ago to around 1,500 today.

Most recently, Tate & Lyle was taken over by US rival Ingredion in a £2.7bn deal in June that ended its 90-year stint on London’s main market.

Wise cancelled its listing on the London Stock Exchange in May after shifting its primary listing to New York. Flutter Entertainment, which owns Betfair and Paddy Power, shifted its own listing from London to New York in 2024.

data.title: Volkswagen to slash up to 50,000 jobs
data.description:
Volkswagen’s shares have surged after the German giant confirmed plans to cut 50,000 jobs as it battles competition from China.

The carmaker’s Frankfurt-listed shares jumped by more than 8pc on Friday after it unveiled the sweeping job cuts, which are the biggest in Volkswagen’s 89-year history.

Volkswagen said on Thursday it would cut tens of thousands more roles as it faces fierce competition from Chinese rivals that are flooding into Europe.

The German carmaker said that the restructuring would be in addition to 50,000 reductions that it has already made since 2024 and could lead to plant closures.

It is racing to cut costs as it grapples with fierce competition from Chinese rivals such as BYD and slowing demand in Europe. It has also struggled under US tariffs and Volkswagen vehicle sales fell by 8.4pc in the first half of the year, while its operating profit dropped by 11.6pc.

News of the restructuring plans emerged earlier this year, but had yet to be approved by Volkswagen’s supervisory board, which represents the labour force and shareholders.

The carmaker said its European capacity “currently exceeds demand by more than 500,000 units”. The new plan will pave the way for Volkswagen to slim its vehicle line-up by as much as 50pc by 2035.

“Given intensifying global competition, shifting demand and technological change in the automotive industry, a consistent alignment of workforce capacity with economic reality is essential,” the company said in a statement.

Last September, Porsche, which is owned by Volkswagen, blamed a decision to delay the launch of its new electric SUV in September on weak demand for electric cars as it warned of a €5.1bn (£4.4bn) hit to profits.

Volkswagen added that it could not guarantee that a number of its plants would be used from 2030 onwards. It said it was considering alternative uses for the four affected factories. Some could potentially be converted into use by Germany’s defence industry.

Oliver Blume, the Volkswagen chief executive, said last month that the company was in talks with defence companies to use its site in Osnabrück.

The new cuts represent about 8pc of the company’s global workforce of roughly 650,000 across brands such as Škoda, Seat, Porsche and Lamborghini.

It comes after lengthy talks between the company, its unions and Lower Saxony, the German state where the company is headquartered. The state is also a large minority shareholder in Volkswagen.

Mr Blume has previously said that Volkswagen needed to rein in costs, which were roughly 30pc higher than its competitors. The company said it was seeking to lift its margin to 9pc by 2030, up from just 3.8pc in the first half of this year.

In a statement, he said that the new cost-cutting plans were “a strong signal for the future of the Volkswagen Group”.

“We are taking responsibility for our entire workforce, for our partners and for industrial jobs worldwide,” he added.

data.title: Richard Branson’s plan to make the Eurostar feel like a second-class service
data.description:
Sir Richard Branson’s much touted plan to bring some of the glamour of Virgin Atlantic to his own version of the Eurostar has been derided as a pipe dream by critics.

Overcrowding at St Pancras, a chronic lack of suitable train-maintenance sites and the inevitable mountain of red tape have been viewed as almost insurmountable obstacles to anyone intent on ending Eurostar’s monopoly over services through the Channel tunnel.

But after securing permission to run 20 trains a day between London and the Continent from Britain’s rail regulator, the billionaire’s Virgin Trains is finally beginning to win over doubters.

Virgin must still negotiate access to the tunnel itself, as well as tracks in France, Belgium and the Netherlands. And it faces a nervous wait for a fleet of 12 as yet untested high-speed trains on order from manufacturer Alstom.

However, a ruling from regulators at the Office of Rail and Road (ORR) last week suggests Sir Richard may be about to make good on his ambition of returning to Britain’s railways after Virgin Trains lost the West Coast Main Line franchise in 2019.

Virgin Trains is not the only operator intent on challenging Eurostar’s 31-year monopoly.

Italy’s state-owned Trenitalia announced earlier this month a €2bn (£1.7bn) order for 19 new trains, around half of which it aims to deploy on Channel tunnel services, while a clutch of other would-be operators are also drawing up proposals.

If those plans come to fruition, competition on the route could explode within five years, which could have an impact matching that of the 1990s discount-airline boom.

Plunging fares may encourage an influx of new customers and further loosen the grip of airlines on routes such as London to Paris, where Eurostar already has 80pc of the market.

Train services from London are likely to reach further into Europe, with lower ticket prices making rail competitive as far as Germany, Switzerland and even Italy for travellers with time on their hands.

Mark Smith, a former ORR and Department for Transport executive who runs the Man in Seat 61 travel website, reckons ticket prices could drop by close to a third.

“You’d be looking at more capacity, higher service standards and fares that could be 30pc lower based on what we have seen with the advent of competition in Italy and Spain,” he says.

“That will in turn drive further market share gains for rail compared with the airlines and make it feasible to travel further into Europe on a single ticket.”

Customer service front and centre

Virgin has so far been tight-lipped on what the Channel tunnel service might look like, with Phil Whittingham, its project lead, saying only that the route is “ripe for change” and that Sir Richard intended to build a “premium customer experience on board”.

A spokesman adds: “We don’t want to ruin the element of surprise, but just as we’ve done with Virgin Atlantic and our holidays and hotels offering, you can expect bold ideas with the customer experience front and centre.”

On Virgin Atlantic, that experience has included in-flight bar and massages, with a shift to focusing on tech innovation in recent years, including free Wi-Fi from Elon Musk’s Starlink and an AI-powered virtual concierge.

Virgin has specified single-decker trains for its purchase from Alstom, with one insider suggesting that they were more compatible with providing a full at-seat meal service than the double-deckers with which Eurostar is renewing its fleet.

Virgin has said it intends to operate an initial six return trains a day between London and Paris starting in October 2030, later increasing to 13, followed by four to Brussels and three to Amsterdam.

That would represent a substantial increase on the current timetable, with Eurostar offering 14 daily services to Paris, eight or nine to Brussels and five to Amsterdam.

The company, owned by French state railway SNCF, said Virgin’s plan confirmed “the huge potential for growth in international rail” and that it intended to “play a full part in that growth”.

Jon Worth, an expert in European railways, says Virgin had impressed with its work to secure access to St Pancras, the line to the tunnel and the last remaining space at Temple Mills maintenance shed near Stratford before Trenitalia.

“Seeing this project through has been like threading the eye of a needle,” he adds. “Forget the rhetoric from Branson about transforming travel. They’ve been very methodical and very clear headed in devising a project that will just about fit with all these restrictions.”

No room for slippage

However, he says Virgin had taken a risk in choosing a bespoke version of a train built by Alstom in Italy which has not yet been approved in France, introducing the “nightmare” scenario of the trains not being ready for 2030.

Any slippage could open the door to Trenitalia, which is viewed as among the most aggressive of European high-speed operators.

Trenitalia’s train order, from Hitachi Rail, adds to an existing commitment with the Japanese manufacturer and will provide guaranteed delivery times, potentially beating Virgin to the market by a year.

Worth says Trenitalia is likely to expand on routes such as Paris to Lyon and Marseilles and Milan, rather than focusing on London.

Eurostar’s switch to double-deckers for an order of up to 50 new trains may also be problematic, he adds, since the Celestia model is not currently compliant with evacuation requirements within the tunnel in the event of fire.

It is likely that a significant number of the new trains will instead be used on the Paris-Brussels route that Eurostar took over in 2022, easing the pressure on Virgin.

Waiting in the wings are Evolyn, backed by Spanish industrialist Jorge Cosmen, an investor in the owner of National Express, the Dutch startup Heuro, and UK-based Gemini, which has proposed running trains from Stratford and Ebbsfleet to avoid the St Pancras bottleneck.

According to Smith, of the Man in Seat 61 website, Virgin’s best bet will be to play to its strengths by offering upmarket food and wine, exploring initiatives such as allowing carriage of bicycles and dogs, which is currently banned from most Eurostar services.

He says: “It’s that hard-to-define Virgin pizazz that people most want to see and they’ll need to bring that to these trains.”

data.title: Burnham faces backlash over Thames Water nationalisation rethink
data.description:
Andy Burnham is facing a backlash from Labour MPs after reportedly shelving plans to place Thames Water into emergency administration.

Backbenchers have urged the Prime Minister to “hold his nerve” over proposals to put the debt-laden water company into a special administration regime, a type of nationalisation.

Mr Burnham has been a fierce critic of Thames Water and has previously said it should be nationalised. He has also frequently promised to bring Britain’s utilities under greater public control.

However, officials have raised concerns about the cost of a possible administration to the taxpayer, as well as the prospect of legal challenges from rival bidders for Thames Water.

The Government is now working on whether there is a viable alternative for putting the utility into administration, with a decision unlikely for several months, according to The Times.

The prospect of Mr Burnham putting the group into administration is looking increasingly slim, according to the report.

The Government’s apparent reticence in bringing Thames into public ownership sparked a furious response from Labour backbenchers.

Jon Trickett, the MP for Normanton and Hemsworth, said: “Privatisation of water has been a disaster. It’s a natural monopoly.

“Worse still, management has proved to be less than competent. Andy Burnham should hold his nerve and stick to his promise.”

Kim Johnson, the Labour MP for Liverpool Riverside, said: “The Prime Minister’s priorities are wrong here.

“Thames Water has been a byword for failure, underinvestment and mismanagement. If we allow it to carry on failing customers with no meaningful consequences, what message does that send?

“This summer has shown just how serious the risk of water shortages is. Public ownership cannot come quick enough.”

The Treasury could face a bill of about £2bn if Thames Water is put into special administration regime, reflecting the funding the company says it needs to remain operational until the end of next year.

Any administration would allow the firm, which supplies about 16 million customers across London and southern England, to continue providing essential services while a long-term buyer was found.

Zack Polanski, the Green Party leader, also urged the Prime Minister to bring the water industry into public ownership. He said: “Privatised water has ripped us off for far too long.

“Sky-high bills. Water shortages. Polluted rivers. Sewage in the sea.

“No more hesitation, no half measures – we need water in public hands now.”

Mr Burnham’s rethink is likely to be welcomed by Thames Water’s creditors, who have been scrambling to secure control of the utility with a proposed £10bn restructuring.

The company has been struggling under a £20bn debt pile and risks running out of cash as soon as October.

Its lenders lined up four new board directors on Monday as part of a potential clear-out of its existing leadership.

The proposed new board would include Mike McTighe, the Openreach chairman, Liz Barber, the former Yorkshire Water chief executive, Clive Selley, the former Openreach chief executive and Dame Bernadette Kelly, a former permanent secretary at the Department for Transport.

Under a 10-year turnaround plan, the new investors said they would take no dividends for a decade or until Thames Water returned to the stock market with a London listing.

Thames Water’s ageing network has been under renewed pressure from one of the driest summers on record.

It has been battling more than 1,000 leaks every week as the clay soil in the ground dries out and causes pipes to crack.

A government source insisted that all options were on the table amid talks with creditors.

data.title: Lime withdraws bikes from London borough after complaints from blind residents
data.description:
Lime has removed its electric bikes from a London borough after the company’s vehicles were accused of endangering blind residents.

The company said it had stopped users from being able to hire e-bikes in Bromley, south-east London, where it was operating without an agreement.

It came after Jason Beal, a resident, said he had had to force his guide dog into a busy road because of the company’s lime green bikes being strewn over the pavement.

Councillors had also threatened to pull Lime’s bikes off the streets and charge the company for the hassle.

Liam Conlon, the area’s MP, raised the matter with Bromley council after Mr Beal contacted him to complain.

Lime’s e-bikes have become ubiquitous in London and a popular way of getting around, but the hundreds of them parked on pavements have been seen by critics as a nuisance.

The company had started offering e-bike hire in the Bromley suburb of Penge in recent weeks, despite not having local approval. 

Lime put this down to a technical issue in which the map for neighbouring Lewisham mistakenly covered parts of Bromley. Councillors said they had “blighted” local areas and caused hazards on pavements.

Simon Fawthrop, of Bromley council, said: “We have already raised concerns with Lime that they appear to be operating without our consent in part of our borough.

“Bromley council have long had misgivings about Lime Bikes and other similar bikes that are quite frankly blighting some areas, where they are strewn across pavements causing multiple hazards.

“The council has not agreed anything with Lime and we call upon them to remove their bikes from our borough forthwith.”

Mr Beal, 53, told the London Standard that bikes parked on the pavement meant he had to walk on the road and listen out for traffic, frightening Caine, his guide dog.

“There have been a number of times the Lime bikes have been parked up or propped up against the tree or left over the pavement,” he said.

“So I’ve got to make a decision to try to take him into the main road. That’s a very frightening experience for myself.”

Lime was recently valued at $1.7bn (£1.3bn) in a US initial public offering.

The company operates bikes and scooters in more than a dozen London boroughs.

It has been blighted by claims of personal injuries caused by the bikes, and said recently that it had set aside $56m for personal injury claims.

Lime apologised to Mr Beal and said that it had suspended bike hiring in the borough until it could agree an approach “with appropriate parking locations”.

data.title: Zoe Ball’s Greatest Hits debut is another shot across Radio 2’s bow
data.description:
Two and a bit hours into Zoe Ball’s debut on Greatest Hits Radio, and it seemed that her former employer, the British Broadcasting Corporation, would not get anything more than a vague sideways mention. There were fleeting references to the “other station” from listeners, while Ball mentioned to her guest, actor Hugh Jackman, that he had also been her first visitor on a previous show (it was the Radio 2 Breakfast Show). Ball is generally on her best behaviour these days. And then, during one of the station’s typically bombastic stings, a wry voice-over came in: “They might have Cox, but we’ve got Ball”. Shots fired!

Ball now makes up a rather formidable daytime roster on the burgeoning commercial station, with Zoe Ball in the Afternoon (a deliberate nod to the late Steve Wright) sandwiched between Ken Bruce’s mid-morning programme and The Simon Mayo Drivetime Show. Nine hours of former Radio 2 DJs – and not any old Radio 2 DJs – every weekday. It would have been unthinkable 10 years ago, but the BBC’s grip on the airwaves is slipping year by year. Commercial radio now accounts for more than 55 per cent of British radio listening. A decade ago, it was 45 per cent.

However, unlike Bruce and Mayo, who both huffed off from the BBC in high dudgeon, Ball’s approach is nothing but sunshine and smiles. The Sara Cox/Zoe Ball quip aside, her first show was three hours of relentless, almost strenuous positivity, with the presenter calling everyone “gorgeous”, stating that she “loved” them and repeatedly using “I am obsessed with” when “I like” would have sufficed. None of this is a criticism. You come to Ball when you need cheering up, when you need relentless positivity and a shot of energy. The outside world is bleak. Stick Ball in your ears and it all goes away. The show’s vibe was summed up by another slogan, repeated several times: “The good times sound like this.” Cue Abba, Madonna, Fleetwood Mac.

The opening record, the Kiki Dee Band’s I’ve Got the Music in Me, was followed by a torrent of good-time bangers, carefully chosen to inspire desk dancing and to make you forget about masked men roaming around Dover or whatever other horrors we were informed about on the hour. Uncharacteristically, Ball sounded nervous, and admitted to as much during a first hour in which she kept tripping over her own tongue. Happily for her, this is commercial radio, so she had ample advert breaks to rein in the butterflies. Midway through, following a welcome laid-back appearance from the old charmer Jackman, Ball audibly relaxed. After that, she found her cruising gear.

“It’s just like the old days, isn’t it?” asked Mayo as he joined Ball for the 4pm handover. It is, Simon. Ball will fit in just nicely on Greatest Hits Radio, which will be delighted with its third coup and will presumably plot another.

The executives at Radio 2, meanwhile, will be watching Cox nervously.

Zoe Ball in the Afternoon is on Rayo and Greatest Hits Radio, weekdays at 1pm

data.title: Primark to offer home deliveries for the first time
data.description:
Primark will offer home deliveries for the first time as the retailer combats stiff competition for cheap clothing from China.

Associated British Foods (ABF), Primark’s parent company, announced the move on Thursday after decades of resisting online retail.

It did not set a date for the launch of the service, which will initially focus on Britain, but said it offered an “opportunity for profitable growth”.

Primark held off launching an online store until 2022, when it introduced a click-and-collect service, and only released a mobile app last year.

The shift to home deliveries is a major milestone as Primark faces growing competition from cheap fast-fashion brands such as China’s Shein.

George Weston, the chief executive of ABF and a member of the Weston family that controls the business, said: “Primark has made significant progress in building its digital capabilities and will continue this through both growing click and collect and by offering home delivery in Great Britain in the future.

“There is now an opportunity for incremental and profitable growth through this channel.”

ABF, which is preparing to spin off Primark and list it on the stock market, said it had bought a “highly-automated fulfilment facility” in Sheffield to operate its new home delivery service.

In a separate announcement, Debenhams said it had sold the automated section of its Sheffield distribution centre to ABF in a £90m deal.

Mr Weston said the UK and womenswear markets remained the primary focus for Primark, adding that trading in Europe “remained challenging”.

Shares in ABF sank more than 8pc on Thursday after it estimated like-for-like sales would be down 2.6pc in its 2026 financial year, compared to the previous 12 months, although UK sales were projected to grow by 2pc.

Bosses said work on spinning out Primark from its food businesses was expected to be completed in December next year.

ABF is listed on the London Stock Exchange but around 60pc of its shares are owned by the Weston family. It is one of the world’s biggest sugar producers and also owns brands including Ovaltine, Hovis and Twinings.

Analysts have predicted that a separate listing of Primark, which has 508 stores overall, of which 199 are in the UK, could see it valued at a similar level to rivals such as Next, which is worth more than £16bn.

data.title: Britain loses third-highest taxpayer to Greece
data.description:
Britain’s third-highest taxpayer has become the latest billionaire to quit the country as concerns grow about a potential tax raid under Andy Burnham.

Christopher Rokos, the hedge fund tycoon and philanthropist, is switching his residency to Greece.

He is the latest wealthy individual to leave the country after Labour scrapped the UK’s “non-dom” regime in April last year, meaning income earned abroad is now liable for tax.

Greece’s own non-dom regime allows people to pay a €100,000 (£86,000) flat tax on all foreign income for a period of up to 15 years.

Foreign residents must invest €500,000 in Greece, through property, businesses or stocks and bonds, to qualify for the non-dom regime.

Mr Rokos is one of Britain’s most prominent financiers, with his hedge fund managing more than $20bn (£15bn). He has a net worth of around $4bn, according to Bloomberg’s Billionaire Index.

The 55-year-old was listed as Britain’s third-biggest taxpayer last year, having paid £330m in 2025, according to The Sunday Times.

The taxes contributed by Mr Rokos last year is equivalent to the amount paid by 21,000 British households, based on the average family’s £15,700-a-year tax bill.

He was formerly a major donor to the Conservatives under David Cameron, to whom he gave £1.9m in the run-up to the 2015 elections.

He also made a record-breaking £190m donation to the University of Cambridge earlier this year, with the money used to open the Rokos School of Government.

As well as pursuing his philanthropic efforts, Mr Rokos is also currently spearheading a £175m renovation project on his 100-bed Wiltshire mansion.

This includes plans to build a tennis pavilion and cinema room at Tottenham House, his centuries-old Grade I-listed stately home.

Mr Rokos launched Rokos Capital Management in 2015, after leaving his job as a bond trader at rival hedge fund Brevan Howard in 2012.

He was recruited to work at Brevan Howard in the early-2000s by its founder, Alan Howard, who had been his boss at Credit Suisse, the investment bank. Mr Howard, a prominent Tory donor himself, left the UK for Switzerland last year.

Mr Rokos went on to build his fund into one of the world’s largest hedge funds through big bets on US stocks.

‘Bad news for all of us’

His decision to leave the UK, first reported by Bloomberg, comes as the worsening outlook for Britain’s economy has led to renewed speculation that John Healey, the new Chancellor, might increase taxes at his first Budget in Oct 28.

Mr Healey said he wouldn’t speculate on possible tax increases in his first major speech on Monday.

However, Mr Burnham has been warned by the Treasury that higher inflation and a possible oil shock from the conflict in the Middle East threaten a shock to Britain’s economy in the final few months of this year.

The Prime Minister refused to rule out a wealth tax before the Budget next month and has suggested the tax burden will have to rise.

He said in July that the Government may have “to ask for a little more” and that there is “some room” to raise taxes.

Rachel Reeves, the former chancellor, introduced a record £26bn in new taxes, including by placing VAT on private schools.

Pat McFadden, the Work and Pensions Secretary, was asked about Mr Rokos’s impending departure on Tuesday morning.

He told the BBC: “I believe he’s a big philanthropist and a very successful person but I continue to believe that the UK is a great country to live in and a great country to found and grow a business.”

Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, said: “Chris Rokos is Britain’s third-highest taxpayer. He has made huge contributions to charities and educational causes across our country. Yet another wealth and job creator leaving Britain is bad news for all of us.

“Whatever your personal finances, wealth creators leaving the UK means fewer opportunities for young people and leaves the rest of us paying more. This is what happens when a government hikes taxes. Our best and brightest are choosing where to live – and they are not choosing Labour’s Britain.”

The scrapping of Britain’s non-dom regime has since led to a string of exits from Britain by some of Britain’s richest people.

Thor Björgólfsson, an Icelandic investor, moved his tax residency from the UK to Italy last year. Italy has a flat tax of €300,000 per year on foreign income.

Guillaume Pousaz, the founder of Checkout.com, also left the UK last year, alongside Nassef Sawiri, Egypt’s second richest person, in response to the non-dom overhaul.

Representatives for Mr Rokos declined to comment.

data.title: Property magnate sues law firm for £180m over Spanish deal
data.description:
A British property magnate is suing one of Spain’s biggest law firms over claims its poor advice cost him €213m (£183m).

Edgeworth Capital, a Luxembourg fund owned by Robert Tchenguiz, is suing law firm Cuatrecasas in a dispute over the sale of Santander’s headquarters on the outskirts of Madrid.

Mr Tchenguiz bought the building as part of a €1.9bn deal in 2008. However, the vehicle he owned the property through fell into bankruptcy, and he ended up selling the property back to the bank for €3bn in 2019.

Cuatrecasas advised on the deal, but Edgeworth Capital alleges the law firm failed to properly advise it about two rulings in Spain’s Supreme Court that would have affected the value of the building.

These judgments limited creditors from claiming interest on certain debts. Mr Tchenguiz owned Santander’s headquarters through a company that had debts at the time covered by the ruling. Edgeworth argued that it undervalued the properties because it was unaware the judgments could limit its liability for these debts.

Mr Tchenguiz claims Edgeworth would have sought €426m more for Santander’s headquarters had it been aware of the rulings. Edgeworth would have been in line for 50pc of that “windfall” and it is now seeking to recover the €213m from Cuatrecasas through a High Court claim.

Cuatrecasas said Edgeworth wouldn’t have gained any benefit if it had been advised of the Supreme Court rulings. Lawyers for Cuatrecasas said: “Almost every aspect of [Edgeworth’s] pleaded case is in issue.”

After moving to Britain in 1979 to flee the Islamic revolution in Iran, Mr Tchenguiz built a property empire with Vincent Tchenguiz, his brother.

Mr Tchenguiz lives in the Royal College of Organists’ building in South Kensington, opposite the Royal Albert Hall. He once owned Shell-Mex House on London’s Victoria Embankment, before selling the building for £490m in 2007.

Mr Tchenguiz embarked on plans last year to launch an ultra-exclusive private members’ club in Mayfair called The Leconfield, supported by Liz Truss, the former prime minister. Leconfield House is the former headquarters of MI5, which he bought for £140m in 2004.

His father was an Iraqi-Jewish jeweller who fled persecution in Iraq by moving to Iran, before ending up in the Shah’s inner circle running the country’s mint. He changed the family name from Khadouri to Tchenguiz after moving to the UK.

Mr Tchenguiz lost hundreds of millions in the 2008 crash, including through the collapse of Iceland’s Kaupthing Bank, and was subject to an investigation by the UK’s Serious Fraud Office (SFO) as a result.

No charges were brought. The SFO later paid Mr Tchenguiz £1.5m to settle a lawsuit brought by the tycoon.

Mr Tchenguiz also owns significant stakes in Sainsbury’s and Mitchell & Butlers, the pub company that owns Toby Carvery and All Bar One.

data.title: Sewage dumped into rivers as rain overwhelms water system
data.description:
Water companies are pumping sewage into rivers as ageing wastewater systems struggle to cope with the return of rain.

Campaign group River Action said there had been 4,600 sewage spill incidents across England and Scotland in the past 48 hours as storm overflows were overwhelmed.

Sewage has been flowing into the River Derwent in Derbyshire for 15 hours, while a spill into the River Windrush in Oxfordshire has been ongoing for 13 hours.

In the UK, a sewage spill is considered legal if it happens during exceptionally heavy rain and only if the sewage is discharged through an outlet named in the water company’s permit.

The incidents in recent days follow the return of rain after weeks of drought, with thunderstorms forecast across England during the bank holiday weekend.

However, Feargal Sharkey, the musician-turned-rivers campaigner, said the level of sewage seeping into the country’s rivers reflected the poor state of Britain’s water system rather than the weather.

Mr Sharkey said: “When there’s the merest hint of rain, copious amounts of sewage are dumped into our rivers and into the water around our beaches. Yet again the profiteering and failure of our water companies to invest is exposed.”

Thames Water spilt effluent into rivers for more than 100,000 hours in 2025, despite it being a dry year.

Severn Trent Water was the only water company to receive a top rating for its environmental performance last year, but nonetheless recorded more than 30,000 spillage incidents.

Utility companies are in the middle of an investment programme meant to reduce sewage spills. Water UK, which represents Britain’s water companies, said the industry was “tripling investment over the next five years to halve spills from storm overflows and upgrade the capacity of 1,700 wastewater treatment works”.

However, Mark Lloyd, the chief executive of River Action UK, said the investment was too little, too late.

“It is disgraceful that funding for new infrastructure to prevent sewage overflows – and for maintenance of existing assets – was restricted over the past 20 years,” he said.

Mr Lloyd added that the recent spillages were particularly bad, as the preceding drought meant the sewage was potentially more environmentally damaging.

He told The Telegraph: “Sewage overflows after long dry periods can be particularly damaging because there can be accumulations of concentrated sewage in the network that get flushed out into rivers that have low flows and oxygen levels, greatly increasing the impact on fish, invertebrates and other wildlife.”

Andy Burnham has pledged to assert greater control of water companies, saying this month that he was “angry” about the industry’s performance, including on pollution.

data.title: Sandbanks residents fight plans to bulldoze historic hotel
data.description:
Sandbanks residents are fighting plans to bulldoze a historic hotel.

The Haven Hotel has stood at the entrance to Poole Harbour in Dorset since 1880, and was one of the first properties to be built on the peninsula.

Once the home of Guglielmo Marconi, credited with inventing the wireless telegraph system, the four-storey building has been a landmark for passing yachts, pleasure boats and cross-Channel ferries ever since.

But the owners of the 84-room hotel are seeking planning permission to demolish it, raising concerns that a building of historical importance is falling foul of property developers.

Keith Ulyatt, a resident, wrote in his letter of objection: “Granting permission for demolition without any proposal of what is to replace it is totally unacceptable.

“It raises the prospect of a flattened empty building plot being in place for years, in the most iconic of local locations... so that any subsequent proposed building would be acceptable compared to the wasteland created.”

Andrew Reed wrote: “This application is nothing short of vandalism, a ploy to avoid the rigorous assessment of a future development application by reducing a useable and valuable asset to a piece of waste ground in the most prominent of locations.”

Sarah Charles added: “The Haven Hotel in Sandbanks should not be demolished. It is a site of significant heritage, and is a wonderful hotel in the present day.

“It was once home to Marconi, who conducted important work for wireless telegraphy, and is an icon of 1920s architecture. It would be an act of vandalism on this iconic Sandbanks landmark if it were to be demolished.”

Marconi, an electrical engineer from Italy, came to England to prove that radio waves could travel long distances. 

He settled at the Haven Hotel in 1898 to conduct his experiments and built a 120ft transmitter mast in the hotel grounds.

Operators on the Titanic used Marconi’s radio network to transmit their SOS emergency signals in April 2012.

Richard Carr, of Property Planning Strategy, who is working on behalf of FJB Hotels, the owner, said the hotel could not be saved in its present form but insisted that a new hotel, as opposed to residential flats, would be built on the site.

“The site has to be used as a hotel, and we plan to submit a new application very soon for an 85-bedroom hotel,” he said. “We are planning to demolish the Haven, which isn’t listed or in a conservation area.

“The building has come to the end of its life. The majority of it is a steel-form building which faces the sea and has been exposed to salt water and south-westerly winds for over 100 years. Parts of it are severely corroded.

“If you run a bath, you get yellow water from where the pipes were made of galvanised steel that has perished over the years.

“The running costs that are just eye-watering and ridiculous. There are people jumping up and down and making noise about what will happen to the site, but if they read the local planning policy then they will see that we have to replace it with another hotel.”

Residents of Sandbanks, which consists of 800 households, include Harry Redknapp and Graeme Souness, the former footballers and football managers, and Sir Peter Ogden, the computer magnate.

data.title: Drivers to miss out on car finance payouts after lender’s takeover
data.description:
Drivers will miss out on motor finance payouts after a lender was rescued from collapse by one of its largest funders.

Blue Motor Finance collapsed into administration this year after facing a £50m bill for redress claims related to the mis-selling of motor finance.

The business was salvaged in a pre-pack administration at the end of July by Hodge Bank. However, as part of the deal, Hodge Bank will not take on the redress claims.

It means many drivers will end up at the back of the queue among the failed lender’s other creditors, missing out on the full amount of compensation they would have otherwise been entitled to.

Hodge Bank was one of Blue Motor Finance’s largest funders, providing a £540m funding facility in 2023. It is understood that none of the bank’s funding contributed directly to motor finance claims that fell afoul of the City watchdog.

Cabot Square, which owned Blue Motor Finance until it collapsed, was contacted for comment. According to Cabot Square’s website, Blue Motor Finance was “one of the UK’s premier consumer motor finance companies, lending over £1bn to over 120,000 customers”.

MPs have called on the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), which approved the Blue Motor Finance rescue deal, to reconsider, given the implications for motorists who were mis-sold car finance.

Bobby Dean, a Liberal Democrat MP on Treasury select committee, said the deal amounted to a “get-out-of-jail-free card”.

He said: “It is disgraceful to learn of firms exploiting legal loopholes to avoid their responsibilities. Using administration as a backdoor to strip out compensation claims while holding on to the profitable parts of the business sets a dangerous precedent.

“The FCA should be protecting consumers who were ripped off. It is disgraceful that they are giving firms a get-out-of-jail free card in this way.”

Blue Motor Finance had been loss-making for years before the redress scheme tipped it over the edge.

According to administration documents, the company had only provisioned around £10m for redress payments by October last year, based on the fact that it was challenging the FCA’s scheme.

This was despite the lender estimating that in a worst-case scenario it could face liabilities between £50m and £70m.

An FCA spokesman said: “We recognise Blue Motor’s customers will be disappointed they’re unlikely to receive all the compensation they’re owed. Blue Motor had been in serious financial difficulties for some time. Without this deal, it was much less likely any compensation would be paid.

“Lenders and their directors are responsible for ensuring they can meet their financial responsibilities. We would take a very dim view of any that tried to shirk them.”

Hodge Bank declined to comment but Richard Saulet, its chief executive, said at the time of the rescue deal that it had protected jobs and was the best outcome for redress claimants.

“By acquiring the business through the pre-pack process, we have been able to secure continuity of operations, protect jobs and ensure that customers continue to be supported,” Mr Saulet said.

“Importantly, this structure also maximises the value available to be distributed to redress claimants, delivering a better outcome than would otherwise have been possible.”

data.title: Developer turns back on housing to chase data centre rush
data.description:
A leading property developer is quitting the housing market to cash in on soaring demand for data centres.

Land development group Harworth said it would cease work on residential sites “entirely” because data centre projects and warehouses are more profitable.

The FTSE 250 business, which regenerates brownfield land for new property developments, said it would “exit the residential sector entirely and accelerate the reallocation of capital to higher-returning opportunities”. These include data centres, logistics and industrial projects.

Labour has pledged to build 1.5 million homes to help tackle Britain’s housing crisis. It has also sought to speed up data centre construction to turn the country into an AI power.

But Harworth’s move suggests the two ambitions are at odds. Although Britain needs more homes, AI projects are proving more lucrative for investors.

The value of Harworth’s land portfolio for housing fell by £16.9m in the first half of the year, which was blamed on challenging market conditions and persistently high build costs for housebuilders.

Harworth said housebuilders were grappling with “rising construction costs, additional policy costs, higher taxes, and a growing array of levies” that had “collectively eroded the viability of many new developments”.

In contrast, its industrial portfolio had produced an average annual return of 24.5pc over the past five years, compared with lower returns from housing.

Angela Rayner, the Housing Secretary, has ushered in planning reforms, including measures to make it easier to build homes and data centres on brownfield land.

Nonetheless, Britain still needs to build more than 1,000 new homes a day to meet Labour’s housing goals, according to Land Value Calculator’s monitor, double its current pace of 547 a day.

Harworth said it was progressing a sale of land for a data centre in Leeds to Microsoft and was in advanced talks to sell a plot for a second major data centre. Four more sites for so-called “hyperscale” data centres have also been identified.

It said its existing data centre portfolio could generate £293m of profit for the business.

The Government has designated data centres as “critical national infrastructure” and has created AI growth zones across the country to boost their construction.

Harworth is battling a takeover attempt from John Whittaker, a Manchester billionaire, who owns a 30pc stake in the business through his company Peel Group.

Harworth rebuffed his latest £583m offer on Wednesday and said it was “unequivocal in its rejection”.

data.title: Starbucks’s shameless makeover won’t fool Britain
data.description:
It was, I was pleased to note, going dismally. In the six months to September 2025, Starbucks – purveyor of obesity, destroyer of coffee – saw its stock price fall by 23 per cent. This followed a prolonged decline and loss of investor confidence. The reasons are multifarious. Indeed, quite why makes for a fun dinner party game. When you’re on to the stickies, and everyone’s feeling jolly, you ask the assembled throng to shout out why they hate Starbucks.

Answers go as follows: “They don’t like paying British taxes”, “They’re expensive”, “The cups are too big/too milky”, “You can’t taste actual coffee”, “They treat their workers badly”, “The design of their shops is abysmal”, “They pretend to be ethical, but they’re just nasty big business”, “The queues are too long”, “They’re too slow”, “There’s too much sugar”, “They make you fat”. And so on until it’s time to move on to the bottle game and do something more fun like snogging.

But you get the point. Starbucks is one of the worst American imports – a company that made us all think they liked coffee, but then sucked us into an experience that became over-complex, expensive and ultimately tasteless on a one-way, high-speed route to obesity.

All of this rigorous and justified loathing did at least boost the UK’s independent coffee houses. For out of the vulgar and sick-inducing smog of Venti Caramel Ribbon Crunch Frappuccinos and Iced Maple Pecan Macchiatos emerged young Britons who embraced local communities rather than fleeced them, who could make coffee that reminded one that at the centre of the story was a bean, and who weren’t just another outlet of the world’s biggest coffee shop chain.

But, annoyingly, like a sleepy wasp buzzing around your kitchen and trying to sting you when you thought that summer trauma was over, Starbucks is fighting back.

It’s got deep pockets, of course, so here it comes with a $1bn (£740bn) plan to reclaim its territory and, worse, do it with the pretence that it’s a natural part of the landscape. It’s doing it with the help of Dawn Clark, senior vice president of coffee house design and concepts, and a woman who pretends, in speech and dress, that she’s some high priestess of morality and taste. In a smock and neckerchief like an Alice Waters of the coffee world (Waters being the earthiest, greatest living US cook and restaurateur), she has been delivering her view on how she’ll make Starbucks a “warmer” experience.

Cafés, she announces, will be redesigned to feel like a “community lounge”, simultaneously abusing the meaning of one word and latching it on to the most revolting one in the English language. She claims Starbucks will serve as an oasis for the “lonely and disconnected”. But we shan’t be hoodwinked.

“The world is coming back to this, being in a place and meeting with humans, not being distant,” said Clark this week, sounding somewhat like she’s been at the wacky baccy.

She goes on to describe how new chairs will help deliver Starbucks’s pledge to “double down on human connection”. Which is the sort of thing a computer says when it’s pretending to be your friend. Of those chairs, Clark has even given them names, such as Viola and Frasca. Starbucks isn’t just a coffee house – it’s a place where the furniture is your friend.

The design heading our way can be seen in a newly modelled branch in Beverly Hills, California. The look is said to reflect the spirit of 1971 when the brand launched. The sofas are deeper and softer, the coffee tables retro-futuristic, there are rugs and houseplants, and the art on the walls colourful and mismatched.

The problem being it looks like a student digs thrown together from the relics of a few dead aunts and a junk shop. A photograph published in the Financial Times, supposedly to show how folk are using the shop to reconnect with what Starbucks calls “an age when an unprecedented amount of life takes place online”, shows a group of three customers, only one of whom has a drink (the other two presumably still waiting), while all three are staring miserably at their phones.

So be on your guard. Starbucks is coming for our high streets to attempt to ingratiate itself with us. Resist. Don’t be fooled. Go local and independent, and let’s see these rascals off our beloved British high streets.
