data.title: Save over £10,000 with our September money makeover
data.description:
Receive free, personalised tips on how to improve your financial situation. Here’s how to apply* or fill in the form below.

September is a month of fresh starts; a new season, a new school year and a chance to give yourself a new start for the final months of 2026. It’s also an ideal time to give your finances a check-up.

You may well be suffering from a summer spending hangover after trips away and days out. Meanwhile, the threat of needing to put the heating on is looming and Christmas spending is on the horizon.

With that in mind, now is the time to make some changes that could leave you better off. From hunting down better savings rates and cutting unnecessary costs to checking your mortgage rate and switching household bills, acting now could save you hundreds, if not thousands, of pounds.

Sort out your savings

Keeping on top of your savings is one of the easiest ways to make money with very little effort. If you haven’t checked your interest rate for a while, or switched your account for years, it’s likely you could be earning far more.

Providers commonly drop rates on old accounts over time, reserving market-leading offers for those who are willing to shop around and switch to the latest issues.

If you have a significant amount saved, a quick check on the latest rates – from our best buy savings pages, for example – could mean you’ll earn thousands more in interest over the course of a year.

For example, say you had a savings account paying a relatively low rate of 0.75pc on a balance of £50,000. Each year, you’d earn around £375 in interest. Move that to a top-rate account paying 5pc and you’d earn £2,558 a year, netting you an extra £2,183.

For those without the time or inclination to move savings around on a regular basis, savings platforms such as Raisin UK and Aviva Save are designed to do the hard work for you. Once you’ve signed up, you can access a range of providers under one roof, allowing you to move your money to a better-paying account without going through another application process.

The trade-off is that these platforms only work with a selected number of banks and building societies, so you may not have access to the very best rates available.

Saving: £2,183 a year

Check your mortgage

Mortgage rates have fluctuated in recent months, with some experts warning they’re about to get more expensive because of rapidly rising swap rates. Therefore, it’s a good time to look for a better deal if yours is coming to an end.

Mark Harris, of mortgage broker SPF Private Clients, said: “The mortgage is most people’s biggest outgoing, so ensuring you aren’t paying more than you need to can make a real difference to the overall state of your finances.

“The key thing to remember is to remortgage when you come to the end of your mortgage deal. Ideally, you should start thinking about this a few months before your deal expires.”

Many lenders allow you to lock in a new rate around three to six months before your current one ends. Doing this can prevent you from being rolled on to your lender’s standard variable rate (SVR). These rates are typically uncompetitive, so staying on the SVR could mean paying considerably more each month.

Say you had a 60pc loan-to-value repayment mortgage with a 20-year term. The difference in the interest you’ll pay could be significant. Mr Harris said: “With the average SVR sitting at 7.13pc [according to Moneyfacts, July 2026], on a £150,000 mortgage, this would result in a monthly payment of £1,175.

“But if you remortgaged to a five-year fix with Santander, pegged at 4.66pc, your monthly payments would reduce to £962, saving you £213 per month. Over the five years, this would save you £12,780.”

Saving: £2,556 a year

Switch your bills

September is the perfect time to give your household bills a once-over – particularly your energy, broadband and mobile phone contracts – to see whether savings could be made.

If you’re locked into a fixed-rate energy deal, or a broadband or mobile phone contract, you won’t usually be able to get out of it early without paying a penalty fee. But if you’re on a standard variable energy tariff, or your broadband and mobile phone contracts have ended, you could be in a good position to switch to a better deal.

This is even more important as energy bills will rise from Oct 1. The energy price cap, which limits what energy providers can charge customers on a “standard variable tariff”, will increase by 4pc. This means a typical household will pay £1,723 a year, up £60 from the current cap covering July to September. It will be the highest level since summer 2023.

Vix Leyton, consumer expert at Thinkmoney, said: “Don’t assume the energy price cap is automatically the cheapest deal available. It limits what suppliers can charge customers on default tariffs, but there may be other tariffs available. Compare your actual unit rates and standing charges with alternatives and check exit fees as carefully as the headline saving.”

Figures from price comparison site MoneySuperMarket show households could save up to £382 a year by switching to a fixed-rate tariff.

Meanwhile, Uswitch says households could save £395 a year by moving to a new broadband deal, and £262 a year by switching from a pay-monthly mobile phone contract to a Sim-only deal.

Saving: £1,039 a year

Review your insurance

By the same token, it’s worth checking when your car or home insurance is up for renewal and getting ready to look for a better deal before then.

Simply accepting your renewal quote might seem like the most convenient option, but shopping around could leave you significantly better off. Customers could save up to £485 on their car insurance and up to £210 on home insurance by comparing quotes, according to Compare the Market.

Timing your purchase right can also make a difference. The best time to buy car insurance is 26 days before your renewal date, according to research, with premiums tending to rise the closer you get to your deadline.

Saving: Up to £695 a year

Scrutinise your spending

Next, look for areas where you can trim spending, and then redirect that money into your savings account.

Ms Leyton said: “Go back through at least three months of bank and credit card statements and look for financial drift, like subscriptions that have crept up in price, memberships you barely use, free trials that became paid services and small regular payments you’ve simply stopped noticing.

“Don’t just check your direct debits either, as that is only part of the picture. Look at recurring card payments, PayPal and, crucially, the subscriptions attached to your phone. It’s very easy to sign up for an app, premium feature or free trial through Apple or Google and completely forget it exists.”

It’s also worth remembering that you don’t have to keep paying for a service while you’re not using it. Many, such as streaming subscriptions, can be cancelled and restarted when you need them.

Ms Leyton added: “If you subscribed to Apple TV+ because you wanted to watch Ted Lasso, cancel it when you’ve finished watching it – you don’t have to keep paying until the next season.”

There are plenty of budgeting methods you might want to try to help you keep a handle on your outgoings. The zero-based budgeting method helps you account for every penny, while the 50/30/20 tactic helps you split your income to cover the essentials, nice-to-haves and savings.

Cutting a fairly conservative £50 a month from discretionary spending would leave you £600 better off over a year.

Saving: £600 a year

Check for switching bonuses

Many banks and investment platforms offer incentives for switching, often in the form of cash.

Santander recently launched a £240 switching offer, while you could get £220 for moving to a qualifying HSBC bank account, £200 with NatWest and RBS, and £175 with Nationwide and First Direct.

Depending on the terms of the deal, you might need to keep the account open for a certain amount of time, but once that’s done, there’s nothing to stop you from switching elsewhere for another bonus straight afterwards.

Leaving out First Direct and RBS – since you can’t use both the HSBC and First Direct switching offers, or both the NatWest and RBS offers – if you were to cycle through all the other available options, you would gain £835.

Moving your investments can also earn you cashback. Until the end of September, you can earn up to £300 cashback for transferring your investments to IG. You’ll need to move £30,000 to get the maximum amount.

It’s well worth looking for these bonuses, particularly if you were thinking of switching providers anyway. But always check qualifying criteria carefully and make sure the account or platform is right for you.

Saving: Up to £1,135

Don’t miss out on extra help

Finally, it pays to make sure you’re claiming everything you’re entitled to. Take advantage of benefits calculators such as those on the Turn2Us and Entitledto websites to help you. For example:

  • You can claim child benefit if you are responsible for a child under 16, or under 20 if they are in full-time education or training. You’ll receive £27.05 a week for the first child and £17.90 per child for additional children. However, if you or your partner earn £60,000 or more, you might need to repay some or all of the benefit via PAYE or a tax return.
  • Attendance allowance can give you up to £114.60 a week if you have a disability or health condition that requires someone else to help look after you. It’s not means-tested.
  • If you care for someone with substantial caring needs and meet the qualifying criteria, carer’s allowance would give you an extra £86.45 a week.
  • If you are the only adult living in your property, the single-person council tax discount gives you 25pc off your bill. With the average council tax bill standing at £2,343, that could save you £585 a year. Alternatively, if you are on a low income or claim certain means-tested benefits, you could be eligible for a discount of up to 100pc of your bill.

Saving: Depends on your eligibility, but claiming child benefit for one child and claiming the single-person discount for council tax would save you £1,991.60 per year.

Total savings: £10,199

data.title: Currys’ turnaround king tasked with reviving tired Boots ahead of flotation
data.description:
When Currys announced that Alex Baldock, its chief executive, was stepping down earlier this year, the response from investors was immediate.

Shares in the electronics chain fell sharply – wiping almost 11pc off its valuation – as markets digested the departure of the man widely credited with engineering the company’s quietly successful turnaround.

Now Baldock appears poised for an even bigger challenge, tasked with reviving a 177-year-old brand that has seen better days. On Wednesday, it emerged that the outgoing Currys chief was being lined up to take the reins at Boots.

The company confirmed his appointment on Thursday, setting the stage for Baldock to try to convince investors that the British chemist could be worth as much as £7bn.

Baldock should be well-suited to the role. He has spent the past seven years proving that legacy retailers can still thrive if they modernise quickly enough.

At Currys, that meant slimming down the store estate, cutting costs, boosting online sales and emphasising its “omnichannel” offering of services, repairs, credit and subscriptions.

Adam Tomlinson, a retail analyst at Berenberg, says that when Baldock arrived at Currys in 2018, “the business was in a very tough place”.

“A major focus initially was restructuring the mobile division, which had become a significant drag on the wider group. He completely realigned it in terms of right-sizing both the store base and the cost base, and turned it from being a problem area into a positive contributor.”

Tomlinson says Baldock’s broader strategy has been to transform Currys from a “product-first retailer into an integrated services business”, encouraging customer loyalty through credit offers, delivery and installation, warranties, repairs and trade-ins.

“What is often overlooked is how much focus he placed on staff and colleagues,” he adds. “He has a mantra that customer experience can never exceed colleague experience.”

Baldock will now have to repeat that success at Boots – a brand which is desperately in need of a turnaround.

Since being folded into Walgreens Boots Alliance in 2014, Boots has endured closures, restructurings and repeated attempts to move away from its old-fashioned chemist image.

Its owners have repeatedly signalled that they would be keen to offload the British business. Walgreens launched a sale process for Boots in 2022.

However, it later scrapped the plans after failing to secure a deal at the valuation it wanted in the face of difficult market conditions and rising borrowing costs. Since then, efforts have been focused on honing the chain, including pushing through further store closures and cost reductions.

Speculation over a sell-off of the British arm was revived last year when private equity firm Sycamore Partners swooped to buy Walgreens Boots Alliance in a $10bn (£7.4bn) deal.

data.title: Guardian staff threaten walkout over pay as paper hails record revenues
data.description:
Guardian staff have threatened to walk out in a row over pay as the newspaper hailed its highest-ever revenues.

The National Union of Journalists (NUJ) is to hold an indicative ballot of members over whether to strike in protest against the company’s latest pay offer.

Union bosses said the move followed a “sustained lack of progress” in pay discussions, branding the latest offer “inadequate”.

Staff are in revolt about a proposal to increase salaries by 3.85pc. While the uplift is above inflation, the union said it did not “meaningfully” address cost of living pressures.

Journalists have also complained about increased workloads under editor Katharine Viner’s Project Berger strategy, which includes greater focus on audio and video and expansion in the US and Australia.

On Thursday, The Guardian revealed revenues grew to £282m in its latest financial year, up 2pc and a record for the media group’s news operations.

The newspaper, which does not charge for online subscriptions but asks readers to make one-off or monthly contributions, reported a 17pc increase in reader revenues to £126m last year.

Revenue generated outside the UK rose 8pc to £115m, suggesting the company’s international push is starting to pay off.

Bosses said growth was particularly strong in the US, where the paper now has more than half a million paying readers.

Despite rising revenues, The Guardian, which is owned by the £1.2bn Scott Trust endowment, lost £17m last year, though this narrowed from £24m the previous year.

The newspaper’s resilient performance is likely to further fuel anger among journalists who argue it could afford a more generous pay deal.

The strike ballot, which is open until next Wednesday, is indicative, meaning the union will not be committed to industrial action in the event of a yes vote.

Nevertheless, it underscores the level of discontent at the publisher. The two sides are entering an Acas mediation process.

Restructuring

The prospect of fresh strike action will create a headache for Guardian bosses two years after staff staged a 48-hour walkout in protest against the sale of The Observer to news start-up Tortoise, led by James Harding, the former BBC News boss.

The sale of the Sunday title went ahead despite the strike, and the Scott Trust invested £5m in Tortoise as part of the deal.

However, it opted not to participate in Tortoise’s latest funding round, which closed last month.

The Guardian has separately outlined proposals to stop using “casual” workers and instead create up to 95 new roles.

However, some staff have raised concerns that the newspaper is preparing to employ an army of low-paid young graduates, similar to the model employed by struggling publisher Reach.

A Guardian spokesman said: “Negotiations are ongoing, and we believe we have offered a fair pay increase which is above inflation and compares very favourably with other employers in our sector.

“We are reviewing how we engage with and manage casuals in editorial to ensure the system is better suited to their needs and our operational requirements. We are engaging constructively with the NUJ as we undertake this work.”

data.title: One in eight Britons to take weight loss drugs by 2027
data.description:
One in eight Britons will be taking weight loss drugs by 2027, a new report has predicted.

The number of UK adults taking glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) weight loss medication will more than double from three million to seven million by next year, according to analysis by consulting firm PwC Strategy&, accounting for 13pc of the population.

This uptick will be fuelled by the approval of a new Wegovy pill, which will make weight loss treatment easier and more accessible.

This is expected to trigger a sharp drop in the sale of sweets and crisps, according to PwC, as the rollout dramatically changes consumer spending patterns.

Those already taking the medication cut their spending on snacks and sweet treats by 70pc and spent 60pc less on sugary drinks, PwC Strategy& found in a survey of more than 2,300 adults.

The latest findings have been released just weeks after the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) approved a tablet version of the blockbuster weight loss drug Wegovy.

This is the UK’s first GLP-1 pill for weight loss and can now be prescribed to adults with obesity.

It means that millions of Britons can access GLP-1 drugs, which mimic gut hormones to regulate people’s appetites, without needing to administer them by a weekly injection.

The pills will soon be rolled out across major retailers including Boots, Morrisons and Superdrug.

However, they are not yet available on the NHS. Before this can happen, the pill will need to be evaluated by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence.

While businesses selling confectionery or fast food will suffer from a drop-off in spending on unhealthy foods, those selling healthy products are likely to see a surge in sales.

GLP-1 users spent 60pc more on fresh food, 54pc more on high-protein options and 40pc more on vitamins and supplements, PwC Strategy& found.

They also spent 30pc more on fitness and an additional 40pc on clothing.

These spending patterns are likely to continue even after they have lost weight and stopped taking the drugs.

More than 80pc of those who had stopped treatment said they maintained at least some of the dietary changes they had made while taking the GLP-1s.

Jacqueline Windsor, head of retail at PwC UK, said: “GLP-1 is the most consumerised medication today. Who your GLP-1 customers are, and how your category changes, will dictate how brands and retailers compete.

“We’ll see consumer businesses reshape their portfolios to manage near-term risk.”

More than a quarter (28pc) of GLP-1 users said they would maintain their current levels of spending on the drugs even if the cost of living rose.

The drugs, which are only prescribed on the NHS for those with severe obesity, have predominantly been purchased by wealthier households, but are becoming increasingly mainstream.

Of current users, 6pc came from lower-income households, compared to 20pc for wealthier households.

Adoption of weight loss drugs has so far been highest among women, who account for 60pc of current users.

data.title: John Lewis turnaround cracks under cost of living reality
data.description:
As he tried to polish a pretty gloomy set of first-half numbers, Jason Tarry, the John Lewis chairman, was keen to accentuate the positive.

“When we put the right products in front of customers, they buy them. We started selling a Dyson toothbrush at £400 last week, and we’ve sold hundreds of them.”

Unfortunately for Tarry and John Lewis, while the Dyson CameraJet Electric Toothbrush – complete with built-in 100,000-pixel lens and intelligent water flosser – has undoubted novelty appeal, it cannot by itself restore the fortunes of the department store.

It is almost exactly two years to the day since Tarry, the unassuming former Tesco lifer, took the reins from Sharon White as only the John Lewis Partnership’s seventh ever chairman. His appointment was meant to signal a return to retail basics that would help to revive the fortunes of the struggling group.

But as Thursday’s results show, the turnaround he was brought in to deliver remains stubbornly unfulfilled.

In fact, the sunlit uplands of sustainable and growing profitability – and perhaps more importantly to staff, the return of a double-digit employee bonus – seem as remote as ever.

The partnership, which owns John Lewis and Waitrose, posted a bruising £124m pre-tax loss for the first six months of the year.

Excluding the first year of the pandemic in 2020, it is the biggest ever interim loss for a business that once regularly churned out profits in both halves of its financial year.

The Waitrose side of the business, under the leadership of Tom Denyard, is delivering solid but not spectacular growth and made a profit of £103m. But John Lewis, where revenues fell 2pc, is the retail ocean liner that just refuses to turn.

There are, admittedly, plenty of headwinds. As Tarry made clear, John Lewis’s performance had been squeezed by a double whammy of unexpectedly fragile consumer confidence and a costs firestorm that includes higher National Insurance contributions and a substantial business rates bill.

John Lewis’s army of loyal middle-class shoppers are feeling the pinch and simply not committing to the big-ticket “discretionary” purchases, such as new TVs. According to Tarry, they are worried about the cost of living – particularly the renewed jump in fuel prices – the effects of the war still raging in Ukraine and Iran and the future direction of interest rates.

Robyn Duffy, a consumer markets analyst at accounting advisory firm RSM UK, said John Lewis was “particularly exposed to big ticket, deferrable categories like home, furniture and electricals – exactly where these consumers are choosing to cut back or delay spending”.

Longer-term trends are not helping. A moribund property market means fewer new homeowners measuring up curtains and running the rule over sofas. The explosion in the number of adult children still living with their parents has also put pressure on the budgets of many customers in their 50s and 60s, who would normally expect to be living the carefree life of “empty nesters”.

Tarry, who has deliberately eschewed the high public profile enjoyed by his predecessor, insists the turnaround is still only in its early stages.

He is also adamant that there is still all to play for this financial year with the so-called “golden quarter” of the year, which includes Black Friday and Christmas. Asked whether he thought the partnership would end the year in profit, he said he was “confident” it would.

Tarry is relying on a ramped-up investment plan to draw back customers. Around £600m will be spent this year.

That investment includes £50m sprucing up tired stores in Glasgow, Cambridge, Leicester, Reading and Liverpool. Platter, a new all-day cafe and bar concept, is being rolled out around 32 stores; a tech-focused sports and wellness department is coming; and The Box, an in-house content studio, has been launched at the Oxford Street flagship.

There is also essential work going on behind the scenes, far from the gaze of customers, such as increased automation of supply chains.

Some have questioned whether it is too little, too late. Julie Palmer, the managing partner at financial and real estate advisory group BTG, said: “Such a costly turnaround strategy across its estate relies on increased revenue, attracting more customers, and increasing margins to foot the bill.

“However, as people have been tightening their belts in the first half of the year, John Lewis remains on the back foot.”

The hands-on architect of the John Lewis revamp, Peter Ruis, the managing director, left rather abruptly last week after less than three years in the job, although all sides say there was no falling out. 

He has been replaced by Will Kernan, who Tarry said today would revel in the pressure of the role, as he has served on the John Lewis board as a non-executive director for three years. Nevertheless, it is a tough gig.

For the uncomfortable fact remains that profitability at John Lewis remains hard to come by. That will be something of a reality check for Tarry, a retail veteran who worked at the profits machine that is Tesco for 33 years.

If Tarry is to rescue his second year as chairman, he needs Christmas to come early and shoppers to be in the mood for spending big. There are few signs of that in the second week of September.

If there is one silver lining, it is the earlier timing of the Budget. Last year’s late November date clashed horribly with Black Friday. The maelstrom of mainly misplaced speculation that preceded Rachel Reeves’s statement was also a disaster for all of the high street.

Tarry can afford to play the long game. He has no shareholders other than his 67,000 staff to answer to, although there is certain to be grumbling if the year-end bonus does not top last year’s meagre 2pc.

The balance sheet is in good shape and the partnership’s corporate culture does not generally include a boardroom revolving door. Baroness White’s tenure of just four years was by far the shortest in the partnership’s history.

But at some point the turnaround will have to be exactly that. It is, after all, almost a decade since the John Lewis partnership made a meaningful underlying profit in the first half of the year. As retailers should perhaps say, profits are not just for Christmas.

Tarry will be hoping there will be many a Dyson toothbrush, as well as myriad other expensive gadgets from John Lewis, round the trees of British customers in December. Anything less will be about as welcome as a visit to the dentist.

data.title: GSK plots £400m Cambridge research hub in push for cancer breakthrough
data.description:
GlaxoSmithKline (GSK) will invest £400m in a major new science hub in Cambridge as part of plans to pour more money into developing new cancer drugs.

The pharmaceuticals giant said it planned to acquire a new 300,000 sq ft site on the Cambridge Biomedical Campus, which will house most of its research and development (R&D).

The new centre of excellence will employ more than 1,000 scientists, GSK said, with its researchers developing new vaccines, HIV treatments and cancer drugs.

However, the move will also end the FTSE 100 company’s 50-year relationship with Stevenage, Hertfordshire, which was previously its main UK research base. Some Stevenage staff will be asked to relocate to another lab in nearby Ware.

The investment in Cambridge comes as GSK seeks to ramp up its pipeline of medicines under Luke Miels, its new chief executive, who took on the role from Dame Emma Walmsley at the start of the year.

The company has been accelerating investment in cancer drugs after it acquired US-based Nuvalent in June for nearly £8bn.

GSK won approval from US medical regulators last week for Jideytro, a lung cancer treatment secured as part of the takeover of Nuvalent.

The decision to open a new Cambridge campus will bolster the Government’s efforts to turn the 100-mile corridor between Oxford and Cambridge into an economic powerhouse.

GSK said the investment would build its presence “in the heart of the UK’s life sciences ‘Golden Triangle’” – made up of Oxford, Cambridge and London.

Earlier this year, Rachel Reeves, the former chancellor, set out Labour’s ambition to turn the area into a hub for science businesses, building new homes and transport links to create Europe’s “Silicon Valley”.

The Cambridge Biomedical Campus already employs more than 22,000 people and hosts treatments for one million patients each year. GSK hopes to build its links with research hospitals in Cambridge and benefit from proximity to the University of Cambridge.

Mr Miels said: “This investment will accelerate our R&D and help us deliver new, competitive products.”

On Tuesday, GSK also announced plans for a major cost-cutting drive aimed at saving £1.9bn by 2029 to fund the development of new drugs. The savings are expected to include job cuts around the world, including reducing some back-office roles.

Alongside the plans for a new Cambridge site, GSK said it had launched 20 phase three trials as part of its plans to expand its pipeline of treatments.

These trials are the final stage of clinical testing before a drug is submitted to the Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency for approval.

Andy Burnham, the Prime Minister, said the £400m investment was “a vote of confidence in British business”.

Life science is one of eight sectors that form part of the Government’s modern industrial strategy.

The investment from GSK comes after its rival AstraZeneca announced that it would pour £200m into its Cambridge site, along with £100m for a project in Macclesfield, Cheshire.

GSK’s relocation to the Cambridge Biomedical Campus means Britain’s two largest pharmaceutical companies will neighbour each other in the city. GSK said it would keep its global headquarters in London.

data.title: Channel 4 to axe 300 jobs in biggest ever round of cuts
data.description:
Channel 4 is expected to cut around a quarter of its workforce in the biggest redundancy round in its four-decade history.

Priya Dogra, the broadcaster’s new chief executive, is expected to confirm the cuts as part of a broader strategy on Wednesday at an all-staff meeting.

Channel 4 is still finalising numbers, but the cuts will affect between 300 and 325 roles, The Guardian reported. A spokesman declined to comment, saying staff would be informed of the measures first.

Layoffs of that scale would represent about 25pc of the broadcaster’s workforce, which stood at 1,276 last year. It would mark the deepest cuts in the history of Channel 4, which was founded under Margaret Thatcher in 1982. It last announced 240 job losses two years ago.

The youth-focused broadcaster is attempting to shore up its finances as it undertakes a difficult shift to the digital era.

It has faced an exodus of younger viewers to streaming and social media rivals such as Netflix and YouTube and has struggled to reverse a decline in ad revenues from traditional TV.

The company fell into a £10m deficit last year – its third consecutive year in the red – though losses narrowed.

Ms Dogra, who replaced Alex Mahon as chief executive in March, has been reviewing Channel 4’s structure and strategy.

The company, which is publicly owned but commercially funded, secured permission from the Government this summer to access the remaining half of a £150m debt facility to ease its financial pressure.

It is unclear which roles will be affected by the latest cuts, but London could face significant losses, as the broadcaster has outlined plans to sell and move out of its Westminster offices.

Bosses have also pledged to increase jobs in the nations and regions after opening a new headquarters in Leeds.

Ms Dogra could also seek to shake up Channel 4’s commissioning strategy to win back audiences. The broadcaster has been spending less on new programming in recent years to keep a lid on costs.

Ian Katz, Channel 4’s head of programmes, will step down next month after nearly nine years in the role.

Mr Katz, the group’s longest-serving content chief, is credited with discovering shows such as Taskmaster. However, Channel 4 has faced criticism for being too reliant on old hits, such as Gogglebox and The Great British Bake Off.

Jonathan Allan, Channel 4’s former chief operating officer, who was in the running for the top job, also stepped down this year.

A Channel 4 spokesman said: “As we have shared publicly, under the leadership of our new CEO, we have been assessing Channel 4’s strategic direction, including a comprehensive review of the structure, shape and size of our organisation.

“We have committed to keeping Channel 4 staff updated in a timely and transparent way, so any organisational change will be shared with them first, and we won’t be commenting on speculation.”

data.title: Dutch shift gold from US to UK because of ‘geopolitical unrest’
data.description:
The Netherlands has moved its gold from the US to Britain because of “increasing geopolitical unrest”.

The Dutch central bank has relocated 86 tonnes of the precious metal to the Bank of England, mostly from New York, as part of its process of “strengthening its crisis preparedness”.

De Nederlandsche Bank (DNB), the country’s central bank, said better distribution of the gold would make it easier to trade and spread risks, and would make it more readily available to use in a crisis.

DNB made no mention of what kind of crisis it was preparing for. However, fears that Donald Trump could impose a tariff on gold previously triggered a scramble to move it out of the US.

Future prices in New York rose to a premium of more than $100 (£74) compared to London as banks, refiners and dealers raced to secure metal for delivery.

Mr Trump eventually clarified that gold would be exempt from tariffs. However, analysts warned that the episode might undermine New York’s position as the largest gold-futures market.

Bullion has historically been exempt from any tariffs because of its important role in the financial system.

“With this relocation, we have improved the tradability of our gold reserves. We expect that we will never need to use them, but we do need to strengthen our resilience and preparedness,” Olaf Sleijpen, the governor of the DNB, said.

The Netherlands held 612.4 tonnes of gold by the end of 2025, worth €72.2bn (£61.9bn). The bank relocated a portion of the reserves between March and August this year.

“In view of increasing geopolitical unrest, DNB is strengthening its crisis preparedness. Improving the liquidity and tradability of the Dutch gold reserves is part of these preparations,” the bank said in a statement.

The UK operates one of the world’s most important gold markets and the Bank of England’s underground vaults hold the second-largest haul of gold in the world.

A recent survey by the World Gold Council found that 57pc of responding central banks stored some gold at the Bank of England, making it the most widely used foreign custodian.

This includes Venezuela, whose gold has been kept in the UK despite requests from Nicolás Maduro’s government to repatriate it.

At the time of his ousting earlier this year, a lack of formal recognition of Venezuela’s new administration meant that the Bank of England declined to release the gold – then worth more than $3bn.

Maduro, the former Venezuelan president, attempted to retake the gold stored at the Bank in 2018 to prop up his nation’s collapsing economy. However, the Bank refused the request because the UK did not recognise him as Venezuela’s legitimate president.

The Maduro government sued for the return of the precious metal in 2020, but ultimately lost the case in the Supreme Court in 2023.
